articles.title: Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
articles.text:
Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- British Ecological Society
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a strange pattern in urban bird behavior: Across five European countries and 37 species, birds consistently fled sooner when approached by women than men. Researchers have no clear explanation for the difference, raising intriguing questions about how birds recognize and respond to humans.
- Share:
Birds living in cities appear to react differently to men and women, and scientists are struggling to explain why. An international research team discovered that urban birds, including great tits, house sparrows, and blackbirds, tend to fly away sooner when approached by women than by men. The surprising behavior raises new questions about how birds perceive the people around them.
The study took place in five European countries, where male and female participants (matched for height and clothing) walked directly toward birds in city parks and other green spaces.
On average, men were able to approach about one meter closer than women before the birds flew away. The researchers measured this response by recording how close a person could get before a bird took flight (termed flight initiation distance).
Published in the British Ecological Society journal People and Nature, the findings showed the same pattern in Czechia, France, Germany, Poland, and Spain. The difference also appeared across all 37 bird species examined, including easily startled magpies and pigeons that typically allow people to approach much more closely.
Why Are Birds More Afraid of Women?
The researchers believe their findings indicate that city birds can distinguish between male and female humans. However, they have yet to determine which characteristics the birds recognize or why they appear more cautious around women.
Professor Daniel Blumstein of the University of California, Los Angeles, who helped conduct the research, said the results were convincing despite the lack of an explanation.
"I fully believe our results, that urban birds react differently based on the sex of the person approaching them, but I can't explain them right now. We used bleeding-edge comparative analysis techniques that showed our findings were consistent across cities and species, but we simply don't have a conclusive explanation yet."
Dr. Yanina Benedetti of the Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, another member of the research team, said the discovery challenged her expectations about how birds respond to human observers.
"As a woman in the field, I was surprised that birds reacted to us differently. This study highlights how animals in cities 'see' humans, which has implications for urban ecology and equality in science. Many behavioral studies assume that a human observer is neutral, but this wasn't the case for urban birds in our study."
What Are Birds Detecting in Humans?
Scientists have proposed several possible explanations for the difference. Birds might be responding to chemical signals such as pheromones, variations in body shape, or differences in how men and women walk. For now, however, these ideas remain speculative, and additional experiments will be needed to identify the actual cause.
Dr. Federico Morelli of the University of Turin, a co-author of the study, said the unanswered question is one of the discovery's most fascinating aspects.
"This is maybe the most interesting part of our study," said Dr. Federico Morelli from the University of Turin, a co-author of the study. "We have identified a phenomenon, but we really don't know why. However, what our results do highlight is the birds' sophisticated ability to evaluate their environment."
The findings suggest that urban birds may be sensitive to human characteristics that people themselves rarely notice. Identifying those signals could help researchers better understand how wildlife assesses potential threats in environments shared with humans.
Dr. Benedetti said: "Urban birds clearly react to subtle cues that humans do not easily notice. Follow-up studies could focus on individual factors such as movement patterns, scent cues, or physical traits, testing them separately rather than grouping them under observer sex. This approach would help identify the specific cues birds detect."
More Research Is Needed to Explain the Bird Behavior
Although the investigation included 2,701 observations, the researchers emphasize that their findings are still preliminary. Further studies will be necessary to establish whether the difference between birds' responses to men and women consistently appears in other settings and populations.
For now, the discovery points to an intriguing possibility: Birds sharing our cities may be paying attention to subtle differences between people that scientists have yet to fully understand.

articles.title: Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
articles.text:
Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Scientists have captured virus-like particles assembling themselves step by step, revealing how a surprisingly simple process of trial and error produces complex structures with remarkable precision. The discovery uncovers a crucial molecular turning point that speeds up assembly and could lead to new ways to disrupt viruses and develop vaccines.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Oxford have observed virus-like particles assembling themselves one molecule at a time, uncovering the surprisingly simple rules that allow complex biological structures to form with remarkable reliability. The findings, published in Nature, offer a detailed look at a process that scientists have struggled to observe directly for decades.
Understanding how viruses construct their protective protein shells, and how that construction might be interrupted, could lead to new antiviral drugs, improved vaccines, and other medical treatments. The discovery helps explain how individual proteins consistently organize themselves into the correct structures despite having thousands of possible ways to connect.
The researchers found that viral assembly resembles navigating a complicated maze, where only certain paths lead to lasting progress. At first, protein components form weak connections that can easily break apart if the arrangement is unsuccessful. This flexibility allows the molecules to keep trying different combinations until they form particular closed structures. Once multiple connections hold these structures together, they become far more stable.
These stable arrangements serve as molecular checkpoints, narrowing the enormous number of possible assembly routes into a much smaller set of successful pathways. One especially important milestone occurs when five larger protein building blocks connect to form a closed pentagonal ring. This is the first highly stable structure in the assembly process. Once it forms, each subsequent stable stage requires fewer additional building blocks, allowing the particle to grow more quickly.
Co-lead author Dr. Roi Asor (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) explained: "A virus has to solve an extraordinary construction problem. Its components somehow have to find the right arrangement among a huge number of possibilities, without a blueprint or machinery directing the process. We can now watch what happens molecule by molecule and see the physical rules that make it possible."
Watching Virus Particles Assemble Molecule by Molecule
Viruses store and protect their genetic material within organized protein shells known as capsids. Depending on the virus, these shells may consist of tens or even thousands of individual protein components. Remarkably, in many cases, the proteins can arrange themselves into the correct structure without any external machinery directing their assembly.
Although scientists have investigated viral self-assembly for decades, capturing the process as it unfolds has been a major challenge. Many of the intermediate structures exist only briefly and appear in very small quantities. As a result, traditional methods have generally allowed researchers to examine the starting materials and finished particles without clearly showing how one transforms into the other.
To overcome this limitation, the Oxford researchers studied an engineered virus-like particle composed of 60 protein units. They used mass photometry, a technique developed at Oxford that determines the mass of individual molecules by measuring the light they scatter. By combining this technology with a new approach for keeping individual molecules confined and continuously observable, the team could repeatedly measure the mass of a growing particle as additional proteins attached.
This approach allowed the scientists to follow the construction process as it happened, effectively tracking the addition of individual molecular building blocks over time.
Co-first author PhD student Dan Loewenthal (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) said: "This method lets us study the assembly process directly, we just take a video!"
Co-lead author Professor Philipp Kukura (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, Oxford University) said: "Until now, much of our understanding of how these structures assemble has had to be reconstructed from snapshots or theoretical models. Being able to both quantify the underlying interactions and follow one particle as it grows changes that. We can see the important intermediate structures appear and deduce a detailed model of the construction process."
The Surprising Trick That Makes Viral Assembly Work
The results help explain how a process involving an overwhelming number of possible molecular arrangements can consistently produce the correct structure. Rather than exploring every possible route, the proteins progress through a relatively small number of stable intermediate stages that guide assembly toward completion.
The findings also clarify why the earliest stage of construction, called nucleation, is particularly difficult and why growth becomes substantially faster after the first stable structure appears.
A key part of this efficiency comes from the ability of protein building blocks to make mistakes without permanently disrupting the process. Weak initial connections allow incorrect combinations to separate, giving the proteins another opportunity to find a better arrangement. When enough components eventually connect in the correct closed configuration, the resulting structure becomes stable enough to support further growth.
Dr. Asor added: "The weak interactions give the system room to make mistakes. Most encounters don't have to be successful: the components can separate and try again. But once enough of them come together in the right closed arrangement, the structure becomes stable, and assembly can move forward. That combination of trial and error followed by locking in successful structures is what makes the process so reliable."
New Possibilities for Antiviral Drugs and Vaccines
By identifying the molecular interactions that control viral assembly, scientists may eventually be able to develop treatments that interfere with the construction of viral protein shells. The same insights could also support efforts to engineer virus-like particles for vaccines and other therapeutic applications.
Co-author Dr. Jack Tan (MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine and CAMS-Oxford Institute) noted: "The ability to understand these processes at the molecular level could have important applications in vaccine development and antivirals that disrupt viral assembly."
The implications may extend far beyond viruses. Self-assembly is essential throughout biology, helping create everything from the internal skeletons of cells to specialized molecular compartments and large protein complexes.
By making it possible to observe these intricate construction processes one molecule at a time, the Oxford team's approach offers researchers a powerful new way to investigate how complex biological structures emerge from relatively simple interactions.

articles.title: A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
articles.text:
A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
A revolutionary laser-powered microscope could reveal a hidden world inside human cells, opening an entirely new window into life and disease.
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Researchers have developed a revolutionary microscope that uses an incredibly powerful laser to make previously invisible cellular structures easier to see. The technology dramatically improves image clarity, allowing scientists to examine small proteins that conventional electron microscopes struggle to capture. It could eventually reveal how tiny molecular machines interact inside cells, providing an unprecedented look at the hidden workings of life.
- Share:
Almost a century ago, a breakthrough in microscopy gave scientists an entirely new way to examine the inside of cells. Known as phase contrast, the technique made previously faint or nearly invisible cellular structures much easier to distinguish. Its importance was recognized with a Nobel Prize in 1953.
Now, physicists at the University of California, Berkeley, have brought that same principle to electron microscopy, a technology capable of magnifying objects roughly 10,000 times more than conventional light microscopes.
The researchers have developed a device called a laser phase plate that could significantly improve cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM). This powerful imaging method has transformed the study of protein structures and helped speed up drug discovery over the past decade. Even so, it has a major limitation: Most human proteins are so small that obtaining clear images of them remains extremely difficult.
The new laser technology could help overcome that obstacle, potentially allowing scientists to image proteins as small as one-third the size of those that challenge current microscopes.
An even greater impact could come from improvements to cryoelectron tomography (cryo-ET). This newer approach combines images captured from multiple angles to construct three-dimensional views of proteins and other molecules. Unlike techniques that study isolated molecules in a solution, cryo-ET can reveal how proteins are arranged and interact within their natural cellular surroundings.
“Cryo-EM has become the new, fastest-growing method for resolving the structure of biological macromolecules, and cryo-ET is expected to show how these molecules work together in their natural, cellular context,” said Holger Müller, a UC Berkeley professor of physics and faculty scientist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory who led the development effort. “But because of signal-to-noise limitations, the majority of human and animal proteins are too small to be analyzed by these methods. The increase in signal-to-noise ratio provided by this laser phase plate is expected to overcome these important limitations.”
An Extraordinary Laser Reveals Hidden Cellular Structures
The breakthrough relies on what the researchers describe as the world's most intense focused continuous-wave laser. Rather than simply illuminating a specimen, the laser interacts directly with the microscope's electron beam, altering its phase to increase image contrast.
This adjustment makes it easier to distinguish small molecules, including hemoglobin, from their surroundings. It could also improve the visibility of structures inside cells, such as the nucleus and mitochondria.
“With cryo-ET, we're looking at small, very complicated cellular material that’s incredibly crowded inside the cell,” said Bridget Carragher, founding technical director of imaging at Biohub in Redwood City, California. “It’s like a forest of trees, and you’re trying to find one leaf on one tree in there. Cryo-ET needs a dramatic step forward in contrast, so we can start to see what's going on inside the cell. That's what the laser phase plate promises to give us.”
With financial support from Biohub, Müller acquired an advanced cryo-EM instrument and equipped it with the new laser phase plate. He named the resulting microscope Theia, after the ancient Greek Titaness associated with light and radiance.
Meanwhile, Carragher is directing the construction of a related microscope at Biohub's imaging facility in Redwood City. Her team's instrument uses two lasers rather than one, building on theoretical research conducted by Müller and his collaborators.
The two laser beams are arranged at right angles to one another and each operates at approximately half the power. This configuration helps prevent components from burning out while also reducing optical distortions that could interfere with image quality.
Both research teams are working with Thermo Fisher Scientific, the leading manufacturer of cryo-EM instruments.
“Theia is the Formula 1 microscope,” Müller said. “It has extra electron optics that give it better resolution than the standard cryo-EM, even without the laser. With the addition of the laser phase plate, we hope that it really becomes the world's best instrument overall.”
The Berkeley team's latest images and technical findings are presented in the journal Science. Details of Biohub's two-laser design are available in a recently posted preprint.
How a Nobel Prize-Winning Discovery Changed Microscopy
To understand why the new technology matters, it helps to look at a longstanding challenge in biological imaging.
Because plant and animal cells consist largely of water, they are relatively transparent when viewed under an ordinary light microscope. Although this transparency might seem beneficial, it creates a problem. Small cellular structures, including mitochondria and nuclei, scatter very little light and therefore appear only slightly darker than the surrounding material.
Scientists have traditionally addressed this problem by adding stains to create greater contrast. However, staining also kills the cells.
In 1930, Dutch physicist Frits Zernike realized that light passing through biological material changes in more ways than simply becoming brighter or dimmer. When light scatters inside a cell, it also experiences a tiny delay that changes its phase, or the timing of its wave peaks.
Although the human eye cannot directly detect this phase shift, Zernike discovered that it could be converted into a visible difference in brightness. By shifting the phase of the unscattered light by 90 degrees, he made subtle cellular features stand out more clearly against their background when the light reached the viewer's eye.
This innovation became the foundation of phase-contrast microscopy, earning Zernike the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.
By the early 1940s, scientists had already recognized how useful phase contrast was for studying cells. They began exploring whether the same idea might improve electron microscopes, which use electrons instead of light to examine structures as small as individual proteins.
Unfortunately, early attempts encountered serious technical difficulties. Devices designed to alter the phase of electron beams often weakened the beam too much, introduced image instability, or reduced resolution.
A possible solution emerged in 2010, when Müller and Robert Glaeser, now a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of molecular and cell biology, proposed using an intense laser to produce the necessary phase shift. Their approach offered a way to improve contrast without sacrificing electron beam intensity.
Overcoming the Limits of Electron Microscopy
Glaeser has played an important role in developing cryo-EM, which offers a potentially simpler way to determine molecular structures than traditional X-ray crystallography.
X-ray crystallography requires researchers to grow crystals of the molecules they want to study and obtain access to an intense X-ray source. Cryo-EM avoids the need to crystallize molecules, but it presents difficulties of its own.
One of the biggest problems is that an electron beam can heat and eventually damage the specimen being examined. This limits how much information can be collected and how detailed the resulting images can become. Covering specimens with metal can reduce damage and improve contrast, but it also makes the images less sharp.
During the 1960s, researchers began investigating whether freezing biological samples could protect them from radiation damage.
Glaeser demonstrated that cooling specimens helped preserve them during imaging. He also proposed using a less intense electron beam to examine thousands of frozen molecules at once, further limiting the damage.
Because the molecules would be positioned at different angles, computers could analyze and combine their images to reconstruct a highly detailed molecular structure.
These advances helped establish the foundations of modern cryo-EM, whose developers received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. During their acceptance remarks, the Nobel laureates acknowledged Glaeser's contributions.
The Nobel Committee praised the technology, explaining that cryo-EM “both simplifies and improves the imaging of biomolecules. This method has moved biochemistry into a new era.”
A 15-Year Quest to Harness an Exceptionally Powerful Laser
Turning the laser phase plate concept into working technology required years of engineering.
Following their 2010 proposal, Müller spent 15 years pursuing the idea, with part of the research supported by the National Institutes of Health.
The first major challenge was generating an extraordinarily intense laser beam concentrated into a tiny area. The researchers needed enough light intensity to change the phase of an electron beam by 90 degrees.
It took a decade to develop the necessary system.
Their solution was to confine a continuous laser beam inside a spherical chamber lined with mirrors. As the light repeatedly reflected through the cavity more than 10,000 times, its intensity increased dramatically while the beam became focused into an extremely small spot.
“It’s 75 kilowatts focused to a few microns,” Müller said. “That’s more powerful than what you use for welding. It's more power than a military laser. It builds up the brightest continuous laser focus ever.”
The team first demonstrated that the concept worked by installing a laser phase plate in one of Glaeser's older electron microscopes.
Additional funding from Biohub then made it possible to acquire a customized, state-of-the-art Thermo Fisher Krios cryo-EM microscope and modify it to accommodate the laser technology.
In their latest research, the scientists tested the upgraded microscope using six different samples that varied in size and preparation method. The laser consistently improved image resolution, with particularly important gains for specimens that are difficult to image using standard methods.
“For the most challenging cases — small particles, bad specimens — the laser produces a very considerable advantage,” Müller said.
Sharper Images of Proteins Once Too Small to Study
To demonstrate the new microscope's capabilities, the researchers reconstructed images of two different proteins.
The first was aldolase, a protein found in muscle that modern cryo-EM systems can already image relatively easily. The second was hemoglobin, the protein responsible for carrying oxygen through the bloodstream.
Hemoglobin is much smaller and lies near the lower size limit of proteins that conventional cryo-EM instruments can reliably analyze.
Using the laser phase plate, the researchers improved the resolution of both protein structures. The improvement was especially pronounced for hemoglobin, highlighting the technology's potential to overcome the difficulties associated with smaller molecules.
“The bottom line is, if you have a large protein and a really good sample — a fresh one or one frozen without bubbles, for example — you may not need the phase plate to get a single, high-quality image. But for a small protein and a bad sample, laser-on is best,” Müller said. “This could fill an enormous gap in our knowledge of protein structures that can’t be crystallized or are too small for today’s cryo-EM. And it will be revolutionary for cryo-ET.”
Protein mass is typically expressed in daltons, a unit named after English chemist John Dalton. One dalton is defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Conventional cryo-EM struggles to image proteins smaller than approximately 70 kilodaltons. That limitation is particularly significant because proteins below this threshold account for about 90% of the human proteome, the complete collection of proteins produced by the human body.
With the laser phase plate, researchers can now image proteins as small as 50 kilodaltons, although doing so remains challenging. Such proteins are even smaller than hemoglobin.
The Next Goal Is to Reveal Even Smaller Proteins
Müller believes the technology could eventually allow scientists to study proteins as small as 17 kilodaltons (the size of the protein myoglobin).
Reaching that goal may require another improvement: using a tightly focused electron beam rather than the defocused beam currently needed to produce sufficient contrast without the laser phase plate.
According to Müller, the laser system should make it possible to obtain contrast directly from phase changes in a focused electron beam.
If successful, this adjustment could double the contrast and signal-to-noise ratio again, adding to the improvement already achieved with the laser phase plate.
Such progress could make it possible to study a far larger proportion of the body's proteins and provide unprecedented insight into how they interact within the complex environment of cells.
“This technology is a step function change for biology,” said Stephani Otte, Biohub’s Vice President of Imaging Science. “We are going to be able to see how molecular machines operate inside the living cell, in context, for the first time. What was once invisible will become visible — and that changes everything about how we understand disease.”
The Berkeley research team also includes Glaeser; postdoctoral fellows and co-first authors Petar Petrov and Jessie Zhang; staff scientist Jonathan Remis; postdoctoral fellow Hang Cheng; and current and former physics graduate students Jeremy Axelrod, Eric Cooper, Ian Hicklin, Shahar Sandhaus, and Cooper Schnurr.
At Biohub, Carragher and David Agard, the organization's founding scientific director of imaging, jointly lead the Dynamic Structural Cell Biology group. Both are co-corresponding authors of the Biohub preprint, alongside Biohub engineer Pavel Olshin.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Honey bees are bullying other bees, scientists discover
articles.text:
Honey bees are bullying other bees, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Anglia Ruskin University
- Summary:
- Honeybees are aggressively pushing wild pollinators away from flowers, with scientists documenting how they chase off rivals and dominate valuable food sources. New research warns that rising temperatures and increasing honeybee populations could intensify this competition, threatening wild bees and other important pollinators.
- Share:
Honey bees are proving to be formidable competitors for food in the UK, and scientists have discovered that they frequently use aggression to drive other pollinators away from flowers. New research has documented how honey bees chase, displace, and intimidate rival insects, providing the first detailed evidence of how extensively they interfere with other species' access to food.
The study, conducted by researchers at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) and published in Ecological Entomology, followed pollinator activity over two years at five locations in and around Cambridge, England. Each site was situated within 300 meters of an established honey bee colony.
Researchers observed insects visiting bramble (Rubus fruticosus) and ivy (Hedera helix), two flowering plants that provide important supplies of nectar and pollen. Both attract large numbers of insects during their flowering periods, making them useful places to investigate competition for food.
Honey Bees Dominate the Competition for Flowers
To examine how different pollinators interact, the team divided flower visitors into five groups: honey bees, bumble bees, solitary bees, hoverflies, and an 'other' category containing butterflies, beetles, and wasps.
Over 93 hours of observation, the scientists documented encounters in which one insect interrupted another's feeding or prevented it from reaching a flower. Each interaction was classified according to its outcome. A 'win' occurred when one insect gained access to a flower at the expense of another, which experienced a 'loss' of feeding opportunities. A 'share' meant both insects were able to access the flower without conflict.
The results revealed a clear pattern. Locations with greater concentrations of honey bees generally had fewer other pollinators and experienced more competition for flowers. Honey bees also emerged victorious in a larger proportion of their encounters with other insects.
On bramble flowers, doubling the density of honey bees was associated with a 14% decrease in bumblebee abundance. On ivy, higher honey bee numbers were linked to reduced numbers of solitary bees and hoverflies.
Honey Bees Chase Away Rival Pollinators
The honey bees did not simply reach flowers before their competitors. They frequently initiated aggressive encounters, driving other insects away to secure feeding opportunities.
Other pollinators actively avoided honey bees in 28% of observed interactions on bramble and 36% of those on ivy. In at least 20% of the encounters honey bees won on either plant, they physically pushed aside or chased away competing insects.
Aggressive behavior initiated by species other than honey bees was uncommon. However, one insect stood out as an exception.
The ivy bee, a solitary species not native to Britain that was first documented in the country in 2001, was the only pollinator observed actively challenging honey bees. Unlike most other insects, ivy bees sometimes defended their feeding spots by chasing or displacing honey bees, successfully competing for access to flowers.
Climate Change Could Make Competition Worse
The findings are part of a broader research effort to understand competition among pollinators and identify ways to reduce its ecological effects.
The results also come as beekeeping continues to expand across the UK. The number of registered beekeepers increased from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 last year, reflecting growing numbers of managed honey bee colonies.
Researchers warn that rising temperatures could add to the pressure on wild pollinators. Their observations showed that competitive encounters became more frequent during warmer conditions.
One possible explanation involves changes in flower nectar production. When plants experience 'heat stress', they can produce less nectar, potentially forcing more insects to compete over a smaller supply of food.
Temperature also affects different pollinators in different ways. Bumblebees and hoverflies are sensitive to high temperatures and may forage more effectively in cooler weather. Honey bees, by contrast, generally become more active as temperatures rise. Previous research found that increasing the temperature by 12°C caused a tenfold increase in the number of honey bees leaving their nests.
Together, these differences suggest that continued warming could give honey bees an even greater competitive advantage over some wild pollinators.
Protecting Wild Pollinators as Honey Bee Numbers Grow
Lead author Victoria Buckle, a PhD student at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) in Cambridge, England, emphasized that the research is intended to improve conservation efforts rather than discourage people from keeping honey bees.
"The aim of our study was not to discourage beekeeping, but to better understand how competition happens between wild and managed pollinator species with the aim of helping to conserve our wild pollinators, which play such an important ecological role.
"We found that most interactions when competing for food were instigated by honey bees and they had a greater number of 'wins', resulting in a loss of forage for other pollinators. Bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies would avoid, be displaced by and on some occasions be chased off by honey bees.
"An interesting exception was the ivy bee, which would win contests more often against honey bees. It is the first time, to our knowledge, such behaviors have been observed and shows ivy bees are able to 'hold their own' in such encounters.
"However, honey bees outcompeted all other wild pollinators and based on our findings, future predicted warming in the UK is only likely to further exacerbate interference competition from dominant honey bees. Therefore, it's important to find ways to ensure honey bees and wild pollinators can continue to coexist, particularly in locations with a high density of hives, such as urban areas."
Story Source:

Journal Reference:
- Victoria A. Buckle, Peter M. J. Brown, Toby Carter, Thomas C. Ings. Honeybees directly outcompete other flower visitors through interference competition on shared resource. Ecological Entomology, 2026; DOI: 10.1111/een.70139

articles.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
articles.text:
NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.
- Share:
NASA's Curiosity rover has captured a spectacular new panorama of Mars, providing its clearest look yet at a series of mysterious cliffs shaped by wind. Scientists have been eager to examine these distant formations up close, and the latest images offer an exciting preview of what lies ahead. Taken at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, the scene reveals striking blue tones across the foreground while morning sunlight illuminates rugged cliffs known as yardangs along the horizon.
Curiosity recorded the panorama using its Mastcam on August 11, during the mission's 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. Six separate photographs were transmitted to Earth and combined to create the sweeping view. Unlike most Mastcam photographs, the images were processed without white balancing, allowing the scene to retain the distinctive colors and lighting of the Martian morning.
Curiosity Approaches Mysterious Martian Cliffs
The yardangs stretch approximately 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern portion of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been climbing since 2014. The rover recently achieved a major milestone, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, a greater climb than any other rover has completed on Mars.
As Curiosity continues toward these unusual formations, researchers anticipate increasingly detailed views of the cliffs. More importantly, they hope that examining the rocks firsthand will help explain how the remarkable landscape developed.
What Mars' Ancient Rocks Reveal About Its Past
Mount Sharp contains numerous layers of sedimentary rock, each preserving evidence from a different chapter of Martian history. Investigating these layers has helped scientists reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams existed in this region of Mars.
As the planet's environment changed, those bodies of water eventually disappeared, leaving deposits of salty minerals behind. Once additional material stopped accumulating on the mountain, powerful winds may have gradually eroded portions of the existing rock, carving out the distinctive yardangs visible today.
Yet the unusual appearance of this particular layer has raised questions about its origins. Its color differs from the surrounding terrain, and its rock layers are tilted in an unexpected direction. Scientists suspect that processes beyond ordinary wind erosion may have contributed to its formation.
"The yardang layer looks out of place. It's the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on," said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "But that's what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions."
NASA Plans to Investigate the Cliffs in 2027
Curiosity is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an investigation of unusual spiderweb-like boxwork ridges. Over roughly the next year, the rover will continue traveling through rock layers containing abundant sulfates and carbonates, minerals that provide evidence of ancient drying conditions on Mars.
Mission scientists aim to reach the bottom of the yardang formations sometime in 2027. Once there, Curiosity should be able to examine the mysterious cliffs using its robotic arm, gathering unique measurements that could help determine how they formed and reveal more about the environmental changes that shaped Mars billions of years ago.
Story Source:
Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Coffee calories have jumped nearly 40%. Sugar isn't the biggest culprit
articles.text:
Coffee calories have jumped nearly 40%. Sugar isn't the biggest culprit
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Tufts University
- Summary:
- Your morning coffee may be packing more calories than you realize, and sugar isn't the biggest reason. A study of 30,000 Americans found that non-dairy creamer has overtaken sugar and milk as the leading source of added coffee calories, helping drive a nearly 40% increase between 2003 and 2018.
- Share:
Americans are getting more calories from their daily coffee, even though the amount they drink has barely changed. Researchers at the Gerald J. and Dorothy R. Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy at Tufts University have identified a surprising reason for the increase: non-dairy creamer, which has overtaken sugar and milk as the largest contributor to added calories in coffee.
The study, published online in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, examined dietary information from 30,000 American adults aged 20 and older. Between 2003 and 2018, average coffee consumption stayed relatively constant at approximately 13 ounces per day. However, the average number of calories consumed from coffee increased from 43 to 60 per day, a rise of nearly 40%. By 2018, the leading sources of added coffee calories were non-dairy creamer, sugar or syrup, and dairy milk.
"Coffee consumption has been associated with several health benefits. However, coffee is often accompanied by the addition of sugar and cream, which can contribute to an increased consumption of calories from added sugar and saturated fat," said Fang Fang Zhang, senior author of the study and Neely Family Professor at the Friedman School. "The more we know about what people are consuming, the better we can understand the link between nutrition and overall health."
How Researchers Tracked Changes in Coffee Habits
To investigate how Americans' coffee habits evolved, the research team examined eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), covering 2003 through 2018. The nationally representative dataset included 30,000 adults aged 20 and older, each of whom completed two 24-hour dietary recalls.
Researchers separated coffee beverages into two broad groups: non-combination beverages and those containing additional ingredients. They then classified the additions into several categories, including dairy milk, half-and-half, dairy cream, non-dairy milk, non-dairy creamer, sugar/syrup, sugar substitutes, and other ingredients such as alcohol and cocoa powder.
Some participants reported consuming pre-mixed coffee beverages/powder, making it necessary to estimate the amounts of individual ingredients they contained. To do this, the researchers used the USDA Food and Nutrition Database for Dietary Studies corresponding to each survey cycle, along with linked Standard Reference codes.
Non-Dairy Creamer Consumption More Than Doubled
The analysis showed that Americans' overall coffee intake, including coffee consumed without additions, remained largely unchanged between 2003 and 2018. What changed was the amount and type of ingredients being mixed into those beverages.
In 2018, dairy milk was the most commonly added ingredient by weight, averaging 21.4 grams per day. Non-dairy creamer followed at 8.1 grams per day, while sugar accounted for 4.4 grams per day. Consumption of dairy milk, sugar, and sugar substitutes showed no statistically significant changes over the study period.
Non-dairy additions, however, followed a very different pattern. Their average consumption rose from 3.65 grams per day in 2003 to 10.5 grams per day in 2018. Much of this growth came from non-dairy creamer, which increased from 3.37 to 8 grams per day. Non-dairy milk consumption also climbed sharply, rising from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.
Other coffee additions increased slightly as well, with an average gain of 0.5 grams per day.
Why Non-Dairy Creamer Now Adds More Calories Than Sugar
Although dairy milk remained the most common coffee addition by weight, non-dairy creamer had become the leading source of added calories by 2018.
On average, non-dairy creamer contributed 18.5 calories per day, compared with 16 calories from sugar and 11 calories from dairy milk. In 2003, non-dairy creamer had contributed just 7.71 calories per day, illustrating how dramatically its role in Americans' coffee consumption had changed.
"We found that non-dairy creamer being added to coffee has now passed both sugar and dairy for its contribution to the total energy consumed from coffee. Non-dairy creamers can be high in saturated fat, which is calorie dense. This could explain the increased calories that non-dairy creamer is contributing," said Yongyi Pan, the study's lead author and a Ph.D. candidate at the Friedman School. "Even though it has been on the market since the 1950s, non-dairy creamer has increased in popularity in recent years as consumers seek plant-based or dairy alternatives."
Sleep, Work Hours, and Coffee Consumption
The researchers also investigated whether coffee consumption differed across groups of adults based on their daily routines and overall diet quality.
They found that people who slept fewer hours generally drank more coffee than those who slept longer. A similar pattern emerged among adults who worked longer hours, who tended to consume more coffee than those with shorter work schedules.
However, coffee consumption was comparable among people with higher and lower overall diet quality, suggesting that drinking more or less coffee was not strongly associated with how healthy their broader diets were.
The researchers acknowledged that the study relied on participants recalling what they had eaten and drunk, which can introduce measurement errors. Because food and beverage consumption can vary considerably from day to day, self-reported dietary information does not always perfectly reflect people's usual habits. The research team took steps to improve the reliability of its estimates.
Co-author Bingjie Zhou contributed to the research while pursuing a Ph.D. at the Friedman School.

articles.title: Tại sao một thìa vật chất trong một ngôi sao neutron lại có thể nặng tới 100 triệu tấn?
articles.text:
Khối lượng mỗi cm3 có thể lên tới hơn 100 triệu tấn và một muỗng canh vật chất nặng tương đương một quả núi trên Trái đất. Sao neutron chắc chắn là một trong những thiên thể dày đặc nhất được biết đến trong vũ trụ.
Sao neutron là một trong những điểm kết thúc có thể có trong quá trình tiến hóa của một số ngôi sao khối lượng lớn. Ban đầu sao neutron chỉ tồn tại trên lý thuyết, nhưng vào năm 1967, các nhà khoa học đã phát hiện ra sao xung đầu tiên và chứng minh sự tồn tại của sao neutron.
Sao neutron được hình thành trong các vụ nổ siêu tân tinh và thường có tính đối xứng. Vì vậy, rất nhiều ngôi sao neutron không bao giờ rời khỏi khu vực vụ nổ nơi chúng hình thành. Tuy nhiên, trong một số trường hợp, tính bất đối xứng trong vụ nổ lại tạo ra một lực đẩy lên các ngôi sao neutron và đưa chúng di chuyển ra khỏi khu vực tàn dư của vụ nổ.
Khám phá này là một trong bốn khám phá quan trọng nhất trong thiên văn học trong những năm 1960. Vì sao xung phát ra tín hiệu vô tuyến rất đều đặn, nên mọi người đã từng nghĩ rằng đó là tín hiệu từ một nền văn minh ngoài hành tinh, nhưng cuối cùng thì khoa học đã chứng minh được ra rằng nó thực sự là một ngôi sao neutron quay với tốc độ cao.
Lý do tại sao mật độ sao neutron lại rất lớn là do nó được hình thành do sự sụp đổ của một phần lõi của ngôi sao dưới tác dụng của lực hấp dẫn, và một lượng lớn khối lượng vật chất được tập trung vào một phạm vi không gian cực kỳ nhỏ, do đó khối lượng của sao neutron là cực kỳ lớn trong khi bán kính của nó rất nhỏ, thường vào khoảng 10 đến 20km.
Khối lượng của Trái đất là khoảng 60 nghìn tỷ tấn và bán kính là 6.378km, nếu Trái đất đi đến cuối vòng đời của mình và bị nén thành một ngôi sao neutron, thì bán kính của nó sẽ chỉ là 22 mét.
Sao xung là sao neutron quay nhanh và phát ra bức xạ cường độ cao, trong khi sao từ lại là tàn tích của sao có từ trường cực mạnh. Tất cả các loại sao neutron đều hình thành khi các ngôi sao có khối lượng lớn kết thúc vòng đời và hết nhiên liệu cho phản ứng tổng hợp hạt nhân, theo đó ngôi sao ban đầu không còn có thể tự chống lại sự sụp đổ của lực hấp dẫn.
Tại sao một vật thể lớn như vậy lại có thể nén lại xuống kích thước nhỏ hơn ban đầu rất nhiều? Để hiểu được nó, chúng ta phải bắt đầu từ cấu trúc vi mô của vật chất.
Vật chất thông thường trong vũ trụ được tạo ra từ các nguyên tử, nhưng nguyên tử không phải là một quả cầu rắn. Bên trong nguyên tử cũng chứa những khoảng không vô định giống như Hệ Mặt trời của chúng ta. Mặt trời chiếm 99% tổng lượng vật chất trong toàn bộ Hệ Mặt trời, và hạt nhân của nguyên tử cũng chiếm toàn tới 99% khối lượng nguyên tử, trong đó các electron thường chuyển động tự do trong không gian cực rộng này, tạo thành một lớp vỏ cứng gọi là đám mây electron.
Nếu tác dụng đủ áp lực, lớp vỏ này sẽ vỡ ra và các electron sẽ bị ép lại gần hạt nhân hoặc thậm chí rơi vào trong nó. Lúc này, cấu trúc của nguyên tử sẽ bị phá hủy do đó một lượng lớn vật chất có thể bị nén lại thành một thể tích rất nhỏ.
Sao từ là một dạng sao neutron với từ trường mạnh đến 10 mũ 11 tesla, lớn hơn từ trường của Trái đất khoảng 2.500.000 tỉ lần. Để so sánh, từ trường quanh các nam châm siêu dẫn lưỡng cực của máy gia tốc hạt lớn LHC chỉ trong khoảng từ 0.54 lên 8.3 tesla. Sự tồn tại của sao từ lần đầu được đưa ra bởi hai nhà thiên văn học Robert Duncan người Mỹ và Chrisopher Thompson người Canada vào những năm 1980.
Về lý thuyết, mật độ của sao neutron chỉ đứng sau lỗ đen, bởi vì các nhà khoa học tin rằng thể tích của điểm kỳ dị được bao bọc trong đường chân trời của lỗ đen là 0, có nghĩa là mật độ của điểm kỳ dị lỗ đen là vô hạn. Tuy nhiên, con người biết rất ít về các lỗ đen, những gì bên trong một lỗ đen vẫn chưa được khoa học biết và nó có khả năng vượt quá kiến thức hiện có của chúng ta. Do đó, các lý thuyết hiện có về bên trong một lỗ đen đều là những giả thuyết và có thể là không chính xác.
Ngoài mật độ cao của chúng, các sao neutron cũng được chia ra thành hai loại đặc biệt, một loại được gọi là sao xung và loại còn lại được gọi là sao nam châm hay sao từ.
Từ trường của một nam châm mạnh hơn hàng nghìn lần so với từ trường của một ngôi sao neutron thông thường và mạnh hơn hàng trăm tỷ lần so với từ trường của Trái đất. Sao xung (Pulsar) là một trong những hành tinh quay nhanh nhất trong vũ trụ. Tốc độ quay ở xích đạo của chúng thường lên tới hàng chục nghìn km mỗi giây và vận tốc thoát ra trên bề mặt cũng lớn tới hàng chục nghìn thậm chí hàng trăm nghìn km mỗi giây.
Trong một số tác phẩm khoa học viễn tưởng, chúng thậm chí còn được các nền văn minh tiên tiến ngoài hành tinh sử dụng trực tiếp làm vũ khí. Nếu hai ngôi sao neutron va chạm với nhau, nó cũng sẽ kích hoạt một vụ nổ tia gamma cực mạnh, giải phóng năng lượng trong một khoảng thời gian ngắn tương đương với tổng năng lượng do Mặt Trời giải phóng trong suốt vòng đời của mình.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
articles.text:
Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Deutsches Primatenzentrum (DPZ)/German Primate Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.
- Share:
Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.
Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide new insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.
Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded
Brain size and the extent of surface folding are important features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.
Scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.
Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.
"We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells."
Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth
To investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.
These progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.
The researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.
"Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets."
The scientists also identified important differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.
Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.
Miniature Brains Reveal Important Developmental Clues
Much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.
"The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," says Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids."
One particularly important finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.
Establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.
What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution
The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.
They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.
Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.

articles.title: Từng bay lên vũ trụ, thậm chí nhìn thấy vật thể lạ, các phi hành gia thực sự nghĩ gì về UFO?
articles.text:
Tất cả những ai đã từng bay lên vũ trụ đều tìm kiếm câu trả lời cho những câu hỏi cơ bản nhất, bao gồm cả câu hỏi cấp bách nhất - chúng ta có đơn độc trong vũ trụ hay không? Và đây là những gì mà các phi hành gia Nga và Liên Xô trước đây đã nói trong nhiều năm.
Vladimir Kovalenok: "Có lẽ đó là một UFO [vật thể bay không xác định], nhưng không thể là điều gì siêu nhiên".
Theo trang Russia Beyond, vào tháng 5/1981, phi hành gia Liên Xô Vladimir Kovalenok đang ở trên trạm vũ trụ "Salyut-6", nơi ông chứng kiến một vật thể kỳ lạ, không thể xác định được có kích thước chỉ bằng ngón tay người.
Phi hành gia Liên Xô Vladimir Kovalenok.
"Tôi rất ngạc nhiên khi nó bay theo quỹ đạo của chính nó", Kovalenok nói về một phi thuyền hoặc vật thể hình quả dưa có hình nón trong mờ, giống như một chiếc găng tay ở phía trước.
Kovalenok đã gọi người đồng nghiệp Viktor Savinykh - người đã xác nhận việc nhìn thấy vật thể đó. Tuy nhiên, cả hai đều không thể chụp ảnh vật thể, vì khi Savinykh đi lấy máy ảnh, vật thể đã phát nổ, chỉ còn lại một làn khói.
"Nó tách thành hai mảnh được kết nối với nhau, hơi giống quả tạ chuông. Tôi ngay lập tức báo cáo điều đó với Trái đất", phi hành gia Kovalenok nhớ lại.
Bản thân Kovalenok không thể chắc chắn về nguồn gốc của vật thể, "nhưng nó không thể là bất cứ điều gì siêu nhiên, vì sau đó đã có thêm hai người cho biết đã nhìn thấy hiện tượng này".
Khi trở về Trái đất, ông Kovalenok nói thêm rằng, "các chuyên gia phụ trách giám sát phóng xạ đã ghi nhận mức tăng đột biến" trong vụ nổ.
Aleksey Leonov: "Một vài sao chổi không là gì khác ngoài các tàu giám sát từ các Hệ Mặt trời khác".
Theo trang Russia Beyond, Aleksey Leonov – phi hành gia nổi tiếng của Liên Xô - là một trong những người đầu tiên thám hiểm không gian, cùng với Yuri Gagarin. Leonov tuyên bố rằng, sự tồn tại của sự sống ngoài Trái đất ít nhất có thể được chứng minh một cách gián tiếp nhờ sự tồn tại của sao chổi.
Phi hành gia Liên Xô Aleksey Leonov. (Ảnh: Getty Images).
"Bất cứ khi nào chúng ở gần Mặt trời, sao chổi sẽ tiêu tốn một lượng vật chất đáng kể để tạo ra đuôi. Theo đó, nếu chúng ta biết khối lượng của sao chổi và đuôi của nó, chúng ta có thể dễ dàng ngoại suy thời gian tồn tại của nó. Trong thời gian đó, nó phải cháy hết. Nhưng nếu nó biến mất, rồi xuất hiện trở lại - logic bị sai. Rõ ràng là, ở đâu đó trong hành trình không gian của chúng, kéo dài 100, 200 hoặc 300 năm, sao chổi trải qua các quá trình mà chúng ta không biết", Leonov nhận định.
Phi hành gia Leonov đặt câu hỏi về nguồn gốc của sao chổi. Nếu chúng được sinh ra cùng với các Hệ Mặt trời tương ứng của chúng - bản thân chúng không dưới 4,5 tỷ năm tuổi - thì chúng đã bị thiêu rụi. Có một số giả thuyết giải thích tại sao điều này lại xảy ra, nhưng Leonov đã đưa ra một cách giải thích khác: "Một vài sao chổi không là gì khác ngoài các tàu giám sát từ các Hệ Mặt trời khác. Và giả thuyết này có quyền tồn tại."
Anton Shkaplerov: "Tôi chưa bao giờ nhìn thấy người ngoài hành tinh, nhưng tôi tin rằng họ tồn tại".
Theo trang Russia Beyond, phi hành gia Nga Anton Shkaplerov đã dành 4 tiếng trên Trạm vũ trụ quốc tế (ISS) và có 3 chuyến đi bộ trong không gian. Ông tin rằng việc con người đơn độc trong vũ trụ bao la, vô tận đơn giản là không thể - mặc dù chúng ta vẫn chưa thấy bằng chứng thuyết phục.
Phi hành gia Nga Anton Shkaplerov. (Ảnh: Roscosmos).
Shkaplerov nói: "Chúng ta cũng chưa từng nhìn thấy Chúa, nhưng chúng ta biết rằng Ngài nhìn thấy chúng ta và bảo vệ chúng ta, đó là điều chắc chắn. Tôi chưa bao giờ nhìn thấy người ngoài hành tinh, nhưng tôi tin rằng họ chắc chắn tồn tại. Làm sao chúng ta có thể đơn độc trong một không gian vô tận như vũ trụ?"
Yuri Glazkov: "Tôi không biết về người ngoài hành tinh, nhưng chắc chắn chúng ta sẽ khám phá ra dấu vết của những nền văn minh chưa từng được biết đến trước đây".
Theo trang Russia Beyond, Yuri Glazkov - một phi hành khác của Liên Xô - từng nói rằng, người ngoài hành tinh không chỉ tồn tại mà đã để lại dấu vết của họ trên Hệ Mặt trời của chúng ta - dưới dạng sao Diêm Vương.
Phi hành gia Liên Xô Yuri Glazkov.
Glazkov tin rằng, 74 triệu năm trước, sao Hỏa và sao Mộc thực sự là một hành tinh duy nhất, trước khi nó bị phá hủy. Ông nói: "Bằng chứng về điều này có thể được nhìn thấy trong thành phần của các thiên thạch rơi xuống."
"Có giả thuyết cho rằng sự tiến hóa trên hành tinh đó hẳn đã đạt đến đỉnh điểm, nhưng chính hành tinh này đã nổ tung và nền văn minh của nó chỉ đơn giản là trở thành cát bụi, lang thang trong không gian vô tận của vũ trụ", Glazkov nói thêm.
Mặc dù phi hành gia Glazkov chỉ ở trong không gian 2 ngày, nhưng ông có rất nhiều điều để nói về khả năng tồn tại sự sống ở đó.
"Có thể đề xuất rằng các nền văn minh ngoài trái đất tồn tại? Tất nhiên, nó có thể. Cho đến khi tính duy nhất của Trái đất được chứng minh, một giả thuyết như vậy phải có quyền tồn tại", Glazkov nói.
"Đối với UFO, chúng ta không thể phủ nhận sự tồn tại của chúng - không phải sau hàng nghìn lời kể của nhân chứng. Chúng ta có thể phỏng đoán rằng chúng xuất hiện do các hiệu ứng quang học đặc biệt trong bầu khí quyển, nhưng một số đặc tính của chúng chỉ đơn giản là làm rối trí mọi người: ví dụ, khả năng thay đổi hướng bay đột ngột bằng cách thực hiện một cú ngoặt 90 độ ở tốc độ cao", Glazkov băn khoăn.

articles.title: Natural compound could fight rheumatoid arthritis at its source
articles.text:
Natural compound could fight rheumatoid arthritis at its source
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- Higher Education Press
- Summary:
- A natural compound extracted from a medicinal plant has shown surprising promise against rheumatoid arthritis. In rats, it reduced joint swelling, protected cartilage, and calmed the immune responses responsible for chronic inflammation. Scientists discovered that the compound works by targeting a specific protein and restoring balance to fatty acid metabolism, revealing a previously underexplored way to fight the disease.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a natural plant compound that could offer a surprising new approach to fighting rheumatoid arthritis. In experiments with rats, the substance reduced joint swelling, protected cartilage, and calmed harmful immune activity. Researchers also discovered that it works through an unexpected mechanism involving the way the body processes fats.
The findings, published in the journal Engineering, center on a compound called obakulactone (OL), a naturally occurring tetracyclic triterpenoid extracted from Phellodendri cortex, a type of plant bark. Tetracyclic triterpenoids are plant chemicals characterized by a structure containing four interconnected rings.
The researchers found that obakulactone helps restore balance to unsaturated fatty acids, which play important roles in cellular function and inflammation. It does this by promoting the breakdown of a protein called acyl coenzyme A thioesterase 1 (ACOT1), using the cell's natural protein disposal system, known as the ubiquitin‒proteasome pathway.
By identifying this previously underexplored molecular target, the study suggests that changing how cells process fatty acids could become a new strategy for treating rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
Natural Compound Reduces Arthritis Inflammation and Joint Damage
To investigate the compound's effects, scientists created a rat model of rheumatoid arthritis using complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), a substance that triggers a strong inflammatory response resembling certain features of the disease.
The animals received obakulactone for 21 days at three different daily doses: low (50 mg·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹), medium (100 mg·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹), and high (200 mg·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹). These amounts were calculated according to body weight.
The results were encouraging. Rats treated with the compound experienced significantly less joint swelling, while the structure of their cartilage and synovium returned toward normal. The synovium is the thin membrane lining joints that produces lubricating fluid and can become severely inflamed in rheumatoid arthritis.
The treatment also improved disease-related changes in the thymus and spleen, two organs that play important roles in the immune system.
Beyond these physical improvements, researchers observed major changes in immune activity. Obakulactone reduced elevated levels of CD3⁺ T cells and CD68⁺ macrophages in joint tissues. These immune cells normally help defend the body, but they can contribute to persistent inflammation and tissue damage when the immune system becomes overactive.
The compound also shifted macrophages away from an inflammation-promoting M1 (CD86) state toward a more inflammation-resolving M2 (CD206) state. At the same time, it suppressed the development of CD4⁺ T cells into Th17 cells, a type of immune cell associated with autoimmune inflammation.
Blood tests provided further evidence of these effects. Obakulactone reduced several inflammatory signaling proteins, including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, and TNF-α. These proteins, known as cytokines, help immune cells communicate but can also intensify inflammation when produced in excessive amounts.
The treatment also lowered rheumatoid arthritis related blood markers, including rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (CCP-Ab), C-reactive protein (CRP), and matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3). The reductions became more pronounced as the dose increased.
Scientists Uncover a Surprising Link Between Fat Metabolism and Arthritis
One of the study's most intriguing findings involved fatty acids, molecules that are commonly associated with nutrition and energy storage but also influence inflammation throughout the body.
Using several advanced analytical methods, including metabolomics, MALDI mass spectrometry imaging, and proteomics, the researchers examined how obakulactone affected the chemical processes inside tissues.
These techniques allowed them to investigate changes in small molecules, map their distribution within tissues, and measure differences in protein levels.
The analysis revealed that the compound helped correct abnormalities in the production and breakdown of unsaturated fatty acids (e.g., arachidonic acid, linoleic acid, and α-linolenic acid).
These fatty acids are important components of cell membranes and can serve as raw materials for molecules that regulate inflammation. Arachidonic acid, in particular, is involved in producing several powerful inflammatory signals.
In the rats with arthritis, obakulactone helped bring these disrupted metabolic processes back toward a healthier balance. This suggested that its benefits extended beyond simply suppressing immune activity.
A Hidden Protein Emerges as a Potential Treatment Target
To understand exactly how the compound worked, the scientists conducted additional laboratory experiments involving rheumatoid arthritis synovial fibroblasts (SFs).
These cells help maintain the tissue lining the joints. However, in rheumatoid arthritis, they can become abnormally aggressive, multiplying excessively, releasing inflammatory substances, and contributing to cartilage damage and tissue scarring.
Obakulactone slowed the growth of these cells, reduced their production of inflammatory cytokines, and encouraged apoptosis, the controlled process through which the body eliminates unwanted or damaged cells.
The researchers then investigated which protein the compound was acting on directly.
Using cellular thermal shift assays, microscale thermophoresis, and surface plasmon resonance, they identified ACOT1 as a direct molecular target of obakulactone.
The binding measurements produced a dissociation constant (Kd) of (6.18 ± 0.26) μmol·L⁻¹ (analyzed by microscale thermophoresis (MST)) and (6.34 ± 0.38) μmol·L⁻¹ (analyzed by surface plasmon resonance (SPR)).
These closely matching results provided evidence that the compound physically interacts with ACOT1. A dissociation constant describes how strongly two molecules bind to one another, with lower values generally indicating tighter binding.
Importantly, obakulactone did more than bind to the protein. It promoted ACOT1's destruction through the ubiquitin‒proteasome system, a cellular mechanism that marks proteins for removal and breaks them down.
This process reduced the activity of several downstream mechanisms associated with inflammation and abnormal cell behavior.
How Targeting One Protein Can Disrupt Inflammation
When ACOT1 was broken down, levels of another enzyme called stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 (SCD1) also decreased. This enzyme helps regulate the production of certain unsaturated fatty acids.
The changes subsequently suppressed two major cellular signaling networks: Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-protein kinase B (AKT).
These pathways act like internal communication systems, carrying signals that influence how cells grow, survive, and respond to their surroundings. When their activity becomes abnormal, they can contribute to inflammation and excessive tissue growth.
By interfering with these signals, obakulactone reduced inflammation and fibrosis, a process involving excessive buildup of scar-like connective tissue, in rheumatoid arthritis synovial fibroblasts.
Additional experiments, including rescue tests and studies using molecular inhibitors, strengthened the evidence that ACOT1 was central to these effects.
The researchers confirmed that the compound's ability to reduce inflammation, slow abnormal cell proliferation, and encourage apoptosis depended on its influence over ACOT1, the arachidonic acid pathway, and the downstream JAK-STAT/PI3K-AKT signaling pathways.
Together, the findings point to a potential way of disrupting the biological processes that sustain arthritis inflammation rather than focusing exclusively on suppressing immune responses.
A Potential New Direction for Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues, particularly the joints. It affects approximately 1% of people worldwide and can cause persistent pain, swelling, stiffness, and progressive joint damage.
Because it is a systemic disease, rheumatoid arthritis can also affect organs and tissues beyond the joints.
Although existing medications can reduce symptoms and slow disease progression, they do not work equally well for everyone, and some can cause serious side effects. This makes the search for additional treatment approaches especially important.
The new findings suggest that obakulactone could become a candidate for future rheumatoid arthritis drug development. They also identify ACOT1 as a potentially valuable treatment target and highlight the importance of unsaturated fatty acid metabolism in controlling inflammation.
However, the results remain preclinical. The compound has been tested in rats and laboratory cells, and additional research will be necessary to determine whether it is safe and effective in humans.
Even with that limitation, the discovery opens an intriguing possibility: targeting the metabolic machinery that helps drive inflammation could provide another way to combat rheumatoid arthritis and potentially protect joints from lasting damage.

Obakulactone Alleviates Rheumatoid Arthritis by Promotion of ACOT1 Degradation via the Ubiquitin‒Proteasome Pathway and Restoration of Unsaturated Fatty Acid Homeostasis. Engineering, 2026; 56: 341 DOI: 10.1016/j.eng.2025.10.029
