articles.title: Why the wires in your ethernet cables are twisted - Engadget
articles.text:
Why the wires in your ethernet cables are twisted
There's a good reason for that arrangement.
Normally, "twisted" and "cable" are two words you don't want to have in the same sentence. And it's true that if there are tangles or kinks in a wire, that can cause performance issues or possibly lead to breakages. But when it comes to the cables that bring internet into your home, there are twists on the inside that are key to delivering the best possible internet signal. Let's get into the science behind why ethernet cables are hiding twisted wires.
A primer on electromagnetism
Twisted pair wires aren't a new technology. In fact, the concept is credited to Alexander Graham Bell, and its use begins back in the 1880s. Twisted pair cables were used for the first telephone lines in the US. Many decades later, they are now the industry standard for ethernet as well.
The reason a twist is beneficial for any type of communications cabling comes down to electromagnetism. When electric charges travel along a wire, they create a magnetic field around the thin metal strand. If two separate wires are placed beside each other in parallel, the magnetic field created by one can impede the movement of the electricity on the other, meaning a slower-moving signal. Twisting the wires together means there's an opposing magnetic field to cancel out the possible impediments, meaning the electric signals can travel at their peak speeds. It's all about reducing interference.
What's happening inside your ethernet cables
Most modern Ethernet cables are comprised of four twisted pairs of copper wires. Depending on how much information is being transmitted, not all pairs may be in use at any given time. But when delivering on standards such as gigabit internet, all four pairs will be active. While the cables have a foil coating around the bundled wires that help insulate the signals they carry from outside interference, using twisted pairs prevents the individual wires from interfering with each other. The issue of wires within the same bundle interrupting each other is called cross-talk.
Electromagnetism also explains why each of the four pairs is twisted up at a different rate. Having variations in how tight the twists are helps ensure that the magnetic field created by each duo doesn't then cause new interference problems for the rest of the batch. If the pairs were twisted in the exact same way, the side-by-side pairs could suffer from the same performance problems as the individual wires in parallel.
Twisted pair wires are standard for just about any contemporary tech cables, so it isn't something you need to specifically seek out if you're replacing ethernet lines at home. But now you know more about the science that keeps you connected and online.

articles.title: LG’s brilliant C6 OLED TV is already $400 off ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
Black Friday is still over a month away, but if you’re hoping to upgrade your TV, you don’t need to wait until November. LG has already kicked off its early Black Friday sale, letting you save on the LG C6 and various soundbars through November 1st. Right now, for instance, you can snag a 55-inch C6 for an all-time low of $999.99 ($400 off), with Amazon and Best Buy matching said price. Other sizes are also discounted, including the 65-inch model, which is on sale for $1,399.99 ($300 off) from Amazon, Best Buy, and LG. If you purchase direct, you’ll also get a free Xbox Wireless Controller and a complimentary wall mount.
LG’s brilliant C6 OLED TV is already $400 off ahead of Black Friday
The C6 is still an impressive 4K TV, even with the recent privacy concerns.
LG C6 OLED TV
LG’s C6 OLED TV offers a few small but welcome upgrades over last year’s C5, including a faster Alpha 11 AI Gen3 processor designed to improve picture and sound quality, along with a brighter display. It also boasts a higher refresh rate of up to 165Hz for smoother gaming, up from 144Hz, while retaining four HDMI 2.1 ports and support for AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, the latter of which helps reduce unwanted screen tearing while gaming.
Unsurprisingly, the C6 delivers the hallmarks of OLED technology, including inky blacks, vibrant color, and impressive contrast. Support for Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, meanwhile, helps make movies and shows appear more lifelike and immersive, while built-in access to Netflix, HBO Max, and the like lets you stream your favorite content without a dedicated streaming device. Google Cast and Apple AirPlay 2 also make it easy to share content from your phone, while Matter support lets you pair it with various smart home devices.
Solid specs aside, we’d be remiss not to mention that researchers recently raised concerns about how LG’s smart TVs collect and log user data. LG has since responded to some of the accusations, saying its TVs don’t continuously record conversations, and that features like voice recognition and interest-based advertising are optional and disabled by default. While LG hasn’t addressed all concerns, similar data-collection practices aren’t necessarily unique to LG TVs, and they don’t detract from the C6’s impressive feature set.

articles.title: Malaysia may extend Waze ban to the public
articles.text:
Malaysia could extend its ban on the Waze maps app from civil servants to the whole country, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Friday. A full ban would come only after officials look at other apps, he said.
Anwar spoke to reporters in Kuala Lumpur, according to Bernama, the national news agency. Officials will check if local firms can build a similar app, he said. He apologised for the trouble caused, but said national security came first.
The government barred civil servants from using Waze on 21 October, The Edge reported. It said Israel could misuse state data and the personal data of Malaysians. The app is run by Waze Mobile Ltd, an Israeli firm that works under Israeli law.
However, Waze has been owned by Google since a 2013 acquisition. Google Maps and other apps remain available to the public, Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo told parliament on Thursday, The Edge also reported.
Gobind said the ban covers only official duties. Meanwhile, the National Security Council urged the public to consider uninstalling Waze, Malay Mail reported. Civil servants who break the ban could be punished.
Waze rejected the government’s concerns. In an email to TNGlobal, it said claims that it collects sensitive government information were false.
“Waze operates under strict privacy policies that protect user data and comply with global legal data protection standards,” the company told TNGlobal.
The government wants people to use TuJu instead. The Malaysian Highway Authority built the app with Prosignal Consortium and launched it in November 2025.
Anwar admitted the app is not yet complete. The highway agency says the app is still being fixed. An iPhone version is due by the end of 2026, according to Malay Mail.

articles.title: 12 Absolutely Banging Proper Watches Under $400
articles.text:
The wonderful counter to rising prices at the very top end of the watch world is that, frankly, things have never looked better for those seeking proper mechanical watches on a budget. Entry-level timepieces keep getting better and cheaper—and this isn't just from newly established microbrands hoping to make a name for themselves, but from the major players, too.
Recently, I was asked to pick a couple of wallet-friendly watches for WIRED's Gear newsletter, and it sent me down a glorious rabbit hole where I was genuinely surprised by superb timepieces well below what WIRED has previously set for affordable watches (the sub-$1,000 bracket). Far from dropping three figures on a decent automatic, you can now get almost anything you desire from a watch for far less than $500.
To check my math and make sure I wasn't going slightly crazy, I reached out to WIRED's wider circle of watch experts with a devilishly tricky, unenviable challenge: Pick their favorite mechanical watch for less than $400, the sort of price where quartz watches dominate. It was a hard ask, but they delivered. Here's the list—all are exceptional value, and watches we'd be delighted to sport on our wrists.
Caravelle Sea Hunter
Caravelle has no right to make a mechanical dive watch this attractive and capable for a mere $300, but here it is. The secret to its timeless look is that Bulova's budget brand sensibly fashioned this modern Sea Hunter heavily on the diver's design from the late 1960s, while bumping the size up to a more modern 39 mm. Elegant and stylish, it's practically a GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watch. But with 200 meters of waterproofing, a 120-click unidirectional bezel, and a 42-hour power reserve, the Sea Hunter is a compelling sports watch. Throw on a rubber strap for diving, a nato for casual (our pick is Artem), or stick with the three-link steel bracelet for a more classic look.
Orient Bambino Version 7 38 mm
Unquestionably one of the best-value automatic dress watches you can buy today, the $295 Orient Bambino’s timeless 38-mm design with white dial and leather strap has been carefully shrunken down from the original 40.5-mm casing, making this piece incredibly wearable (both in these smaller watch times and when case sizes inevitably get larger again.) You can view the automatic Japanese movement through the exhibition case back, and there's even 30 meters of water resistance—not that you should be swimming with such a watch. Want something less traditional? Go for the pink dial with a stainless steel bracelet.
Brew Metric Lite Retro
This new smaller take on Brew's original Metric Retro is the choice of Mike Christensen, British GQ's lifestyle director and watch editor. Cashing in on the current trend for very small watches, Mike loves that this 30-mm piece is wearable for both men and women. “This li'l Brew number is so retro they decided to call it exactly that,” he says. At just $375, the stainless steel Metric Lite Retro, complete with a matching bracelet, uses an automatic movement visible through the open caseback. It has 50 meters of water resistance, and even sapphire crystal atop the striking dial. Proper retro charm that's forgiving on the bank balance.
Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound
Chris Hall, a watch expert who writes for WIRED, The New York Times, Financial Times, and others, as well as his excellent The Fourth Wheel Substack, recommends the Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound at $259. “It was the model that marked Timex’s return to mechanical watches about a decade ago, and unlike so many watches at this level, it isn’t a rip-off of something else: It’s a tribute to one of Timex’s own designs,” Hall says. “It’s small, quirky, and very much its own thing. Never mind the mechanics, getting real personality and credibility at this price is what’s really impressive.” At 34 mm on a leather strap, the design feels pure, and the 30-meter water resistance is a bonus.
Sea-Gull 1963 “International Edition”
Looking a little further afield can often pay off in the watch world. A prime example is the Sea-Gull 1963, a hand-wound mechanical chronograph based on a vintage pilot's timepiece originally built for the Chinese Air Force back in 1961. Many call this watch the gateway drug to watch collecting, but there are a few different versions. Here we've gone for the “International Edition,” which seems to be a budget model of the 1963 Sea-Gull, as it sells alternative iterations for more on its own website. The design is faithful (including the ST1901 movement), the 38-mm size is perfect, and you can't argue with the unfathomably low $269 price.
Baltic HMS
Founded in 2016 by Etienne Malec and debuting on Kickstarter in 2017, this French micro-brand was inspired by the watch collection Malec inherited from his late father, whose family hailed from northern Poland near the Baltic Sea. The brand has quickly become a darling of watch reviewers, so it's no surprise that two of WIRED's watch experts have chosen the 1940s-inspired three-hand HMS (cheating ever so slightly as the HMS clocks in at $430).
Robin Swithinbank, who writes on watches for The New York Times, Financial Times, and Business of Fashion, and hosts the Luxury Society Podcast, has been won over by the 38-mm HMS 002 Silver (above right). “At any price, I like my watches simple, legible, and hardwired with the kind of style that never dies. Baltic absolutely nailed it with this,” he says. Powered by an automatic Miyota 8315 movement with a 60-hour power reserve, it also has 50 meters of water resistance.
Tim Vaux, who writes for both Hodinkee and British GQ about watches, prefers the HMS 003 Salmon (above left). It's smaller than the 002 at 36.5 mm, but still uses the Miyota 8315 movement. “In 2026, there’s no need to look at the household names anymore. The HMS 003 has one of the most classically configured dials you’ll find at any price,” Vaux says. “Walk into a room wearing this and nods of approval will come from all angles. With the Salmon dial, you can’t go wrong.”
Bulova A-11 Hack Watch
As Caravelle's big brother, Bulova has appeared in our bargain watch roundups before. Still, this time, Felix Scholz, editor-in-chief of Revolution Australia and cohost of OT: The Podcast, chose the A-11 Hack Watch, on sale for just $357. “Military watches hold a special place in the hearts of watch enthusiasts,” Scholz says. “And while they might not be rare or intrinsically valuable, the hacking watches produced by numerous American makers during the Second World War are among the greatest.”
Legible and functional, Scholz says such pieces are a true slice of history, and that Bulova is one of the historic manufacturers of this type. “The A-11 Hack captures the spirit, but the less martial blue dial feels contemporary, and doesn't make you look like you're LARPing as a reenactor.”
Citizen Tsuyosa
Pickings are admittedly slim for genuine automatic GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watches under $400, but take a look at the $396 Citizen Tsuyosa with its classic black dial and integrated stainless steel bracelet. It features a 40-mm case, 50 meters of water resistance, sapphire crystal, 42-hour power reserve, and a 3 o’clock date window that will see you from beach to boardroom. If black is too serious, Citizen offers several dial hues (gold and green is a nice combo).
WIRED's top pick, however, is the new, more wearable 37-mm range conveniently on sale right now at just under our $400 target. If you venture above $600, park Citizen and go for the Lorier Falcon or Traska Commuter 36 instead.
Vostok Amphibia
WIRED watch expert Laura McCreddie-Doak has seen our Chinese chrono option and upped the ante with this Russian dive watch. Vostok traces back to the Soviet Union's Chistopol Watch Factory, a supplier to the USSR Ministry of Defense during World War II. This Amphibia 420269 (there are many, many other models) has a 2416B automatic movement that offers a 31-hour power reserve. Bafflingly just $151 on a steel bracelet, it's rated for 200 meters of water resistance, thanks to its unique, pressure-tightening case design. “This watch needs no other justification for inclusion on this list other than it was worn by Bill Murray as Jacques Cousteau-alike Steve Zissou in Wes Anderson’s The Life Aquatic,” says McCreddie-Doak.
Seiko 5 Sports
Finally, we come to the almost inevitable inclusion of the Seiko 5 Sports automatic. The familiar and affordable Seiko 5 Sports line began in 1968 as a tougher, sportier evolution of the 1963 Seiko Sportsmatic 5. The lineup is still going strong with dozens of variants plus a back catalog of thousands. That explains why, for the second time on this list, two of our experts chose the 5 Sports.
WIRED watch writer and author Josh Sims says the Seiko 5 Sports “is the MPV of watches: dependable, rugged, adaptable, as happy in the city as out of it. For my money—and this really is a lot of watch for, relatively, not a lot of money—it also has the cool of not being Swiss. Seiko isn’t just a giant of Japanese watchmaking; it’s a giant of watchmaking that deserves more r-e-s-p-e-c-t, and remains as relevant as ever.” Sims has gone for the SNSX Series that starts at $385.
Holly Ross, as executive editor of Vanity Fair’s On Time watch supplement, has gone for the Seiko 5 SRPE71 (pictured above), a model that's not new but still available if you look. “What is not to love about this chic, timeless, durable, and mechanical Seiko 5? And for a neat $320, it makes it even more desirable.”

articles.title: Dự toán ngân sách năm 2027: Tổng thu hơn 3,3 triệu tỷ, chi hơn 4 triệu tỷ đồng
articles.text:
Thu ngân sách tăng 9,1%, chi hơn 4 triệu tỷ đồng
Theo Báo cáo công khai dự toán ngân sách nhà nước (NSNN) năm 2027 Chính phủ trình Quốc hội do Bộ Tài chính biên soạn, tổng thu NSNN năm 2027 dự kiến đạt 3.334,3 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng khoảng 9,1% so với ước thực hiện năm 2026. Tỷ lệ huy động vào ngân sách dự kiến khoảng 20,2% GDP.
Trong đó, thu nội địa dự kiến đạt 2.949,5 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 10% so với ước thực hiện năm 2026, chiếm 88,5% tổng thu ngân sách. Thu từ hoạt động xuất nhập khẩu dự kiến đạt 531 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 6%.
Thu dầu thô được dự báo đạt 52 nghìn tỷ đồng, bằng 83,5% mức ước thực hiện năm 2026, trên cơ sở giá dầu dự kiến khoảng 75 USD/thùng và sản lượng kế hoạch 8,5 triệu tấn. Khoản hoàn thuế giá trị gia tăng dự kiến khoảng 207,2 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 5,1%; thu viện trợ đạt khoảng 9 nghìn tỷ đồng.
Bộ Tài chính cho biết, dự toán thu được xây dựng trên cơ sở chính sách thuế và các khoản thu ngân sách hiện hành, đồng thời tiếp tục thực hiện một số chính sách miễn, giảm thuế để hỗ trợ sản xuất, kinh doanh. Định hướng là cơ cấu lại nguồn thu theo hướng bền vững hơn, tăng tỷ trọng thu nội địa và giảm phụ thuộc vào những nguồn thu chịu tác động từ bên ngoài.
Ở chiều chi, tổng chi NSNN năm 2027 dự kiến đạt 4.074,3 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 915,2 nghìn tỷ đồng so với dự toán năm 2026.
Trong cơ cấu chi, ngân sách dành khoảng 1.756 nghìn tỷ đồng cho đầu tư phát triển, chiếm 43% tổng chi, cao hơn mức 35,5% trong dự toán năm 2026.
Chi thường xuyên, bao gồm chi cải cách tiền lương, dự kiến ở mức 2.061,3 nghìn tỷ đồng, tương đương 50,6% tổng chi, giảm tỷ trọng so với mức 57,3% của năm trước.
Đối với ngân sách trung ương, tổng chi dự kiến khoảng 1.955,7 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 438,6 nghìn tỷ đồng. Trong đó, chi đầu tư phát triển khoảng 757,2 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 287,2 nghìn tỷ đồng so với dự toán năm 2026.
Riêng chi đầu tư công được bố trí 690 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 260 nghìn tỷ đồng, tập trung cho các công trình, dự án quan trọng quốc gia và những dự án thúc đẩy tăng trưởng kinh tế trong kế hoạch đầu tư công trung hạn giai đoạn 2026-2030.
Chi đầu tư phát triển khác dự kiến đạt 67,2 nghìn tỷ đồng, gồm các khoản hỗ trợ đầu tư, bù giá bao tiêu dự án Nhà máy lọc hóa dầu Nghi Sơn và bổ sung vốn điều lệ cho một số doanh nghiệp, ngân hàng.
Chi thường xuyên của ngân sách trung ương, bao gồm cải cách tiền lương, dự kiến đạt 980,9 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 120,5 nghìn tỷ đồng. Trong đó, khoảng 80,4 nghìn tỷ đồng được bố trí cho cải cách tiền lương, thu nhập khu vực công và bổ sung nguồn tích lũy cải cách tiền lương.
Đối với ngân sách địa phương, tổng chi dự kiến khoảng 2.118,6 nghìn tỷ đồng, tăng 476,6 nghìn tỷ đồng. Trong đó, chi đầu tư phát triển đạt khoảng 998,8 nghìn tỷ đồng, còn chi thường xuyên khoảng 1.080,3 nghìn tỷ đồng.
Bội chi ngân sách khoảng 4,5% GDP
Về các chỉ tiêu kinh tế - xã hội chủ yếu năm 2027, dự toán được xây dựng theo mục tiêu tăng trưởng GDP từ 10% trở lên, GDP bình quân đầu người khoảng 6.100 USD, CPI tăng khoảng 4,5%; kim ngạch xuất khẩu hàng hóa tăng 15%, nhập khẩu tăng 12%; tổng vốn đầu tư thực hiện toàn xã hội đạt 36-38% GDP và năng suất lao động tăng 8,6%.
Về bội chi, dự toán năm 2027 ở mức khoảng 740 nghìn tỷ đồng, tương đương 4,5% GDP, tăng 134,2 nghìn tỷ đồng so với dự toán năm 2026. Trong đó, bội chi ngân sách trung ương khoảng 588,8 nghìn tỷ đồng và bội chi ngân sách địa phương khoảng 150,8 nghìn tỷ đồng.
Đến cuối năm 2027, nợ công được dự báo ở mức 34-35% GDP; nợ Chính phủ khoảng 33-34% GDP và nợ nước ngoài của quốc gia khoảng 30-31% GDP.
Để bảo đảm an toàn tài chính quốc gia, Chính phủ định hướng kiểm soát các chỉ tiêu an toàn nợ, quản lý rủi ro, chủ động và linh hoạt huy động vốn gắn với ổn định kinh tế vĩ mô, đồng thời bảo đảm trả nợ đầy đủ, đúng hạn và nâng cao hiệu quả sử dụng vốn vay.
Ngân sách cũng dự kiến dành khoảng 30 nghìn tỷ đồng làm nguồn dự phòng để chủ động điều hành khi tình hình kinh tế - xã hội biến động hoặc thu ngân sách không đạt dự toán.
Bên cạnh đó, dự toán yêu cầu tiết kiệm ngay từ khâu phân bổ ngân sách đầu năm, gồm 5% chi đầu tư công để bổ sung cho các dự án trọng điểm, cấp thiết và 10% chi thường xuyên, ngoài phần tiết kiệm tạo nguồn cải cách tiền lương, để bổ sung nguồn chi an sinh xã hội.
Định hướng điều hành ngân sách là phối hợp hợp lý giữa chính sách tài khóa, tiền tệ và các chính sách vĩ mô khác; ưu tiên nguồn lực cho đầu tư phát triển, các công trình chiến lược, an sinh xã hội, quốc phòng, an ninh, đồng thời tăng cường kỷ luật tài khóa và nâng cao hiệu quả sử dụng NSNN.

articles.title: The UK is investing $134 million into an AI Biosecurity Lab - Engadget
articles.text:
The UK is investing $134 million into an AI Biosecurity Lab
OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepSeek are supporting the initiative.
The UK government has established the AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) as part of its National AI Biosecurity Initiative. It has committed £100 million ($134 million) in funding to the project, which will also be supported by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepSeek. The AI Biosecurity Lab will bring in experts in biosecurity and life sciences who will work with frontier AI to detect biological threats and accelerate the development of vaccines and medical treatments. It will operate as an independent, non-profit organization, but it will also team up with public-sector organizations and academic institutions.
In its announcement, the UK government says AI systems are "creating unprecedented opportunities for scientific discovery," but they're also creating "new biological risks and could lower barriers to harmful activity." An AI research lab in California, for instance, recently claimed to have created a virus with AI, which it had then administered into a human patient. The virus was created to infect antibiotic-resistant bacteria rather than for anything nefarious, but the lab's work demonstrates how frontier AI can be used for biotech purposes. "AIBL's cutting-edge research will strengthen UK and global resilience to a wide range of biological risks, including those enabled by advances in AI," the UK government said.
Kanishka Narayan, Britain's AI minister, said the lab "will be a major new global institution, bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats and ensure Britain leads the world in AI safety and security."
OpenAI is backing the initiative by providing £100 million in credits that the lab can use to access its most advanced models and computing infrastructure. Meanwhile, Anthropic will provide the lab with £100 million model credits. The lab will also collaborate with Google DeepMind and UK AI life sciences company Basecamp Research. DeepMind's biosecurity experts will work on research with the lab, as well as provide access to frontier Gemini models, while Basecamp will provide it with AI-biology models and its technical expertise when it comes to biosecurity challenges.

articles.title: Kids Will Love This Interactive Wooden Soundstage
articles.text:
Most parents worry about exposing their kids to too much screen time, but it can be tough to find alternatives that children find entertaining and that might be beneficial. Enter Qubitunes, a screen-free play stage and speaker for kids. Content comes in wooden cartridges that you slot in the top, and kids can place wooden character pieces on the circular soundstage, divided into four sections, to change the audio it plays.
This seemingly simple design allows for interactive stories that change based on the characters and spots your kids choose, music that can be layered up with different instruments, and themed games and quizzes. I’m a huge fan of Qubitunes, and it has a deserving place in my guides to the best STEM toys and speakers for kids. As Black Friday and gifting season approaches, the Qubitunes starter kit is one toy to keep an eye on for discounts.
I played with Qubitunes for hours when it arrived and really enjoyed it. The stereo speakers are decent, there's a headphone port, and it can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. It has since gone into my wife’s classroom, and it’s usually the first thing picked when kids have finished their work and it’s choosing time. It’s very popular with 7- and 8-year-olds, but kids aged 3 years and up (all the way up to adults) will potentially get a kick out of this.
There is a caveat: the need to purchase content separately. These add-ons cost between $10 and $20 each. Stories, games, and other options come in wooden blocks that slot into the device so you can download the content. You need a Wi-Fi connection for the initial content download and firmware updates, but then you can play offline. They usually come with three or four character blocks and a labelled bag to keep them in.
My top pick is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. There are also stories about quirky characters, such as The Groblies ($20), a fun cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients, and various themed soundscapes and quizzes. I prefer activities where there’s some creativity or a learning game involved, but the stories and soundscapes are good for very young kids. The interactive nature of these sets elevates the experience beyond passive listening and provides replay value, as kids experiment to discover what happens when they move and replace pieces on the stage.
Qubs has also recently released a Maestro expansion ($10) with four new composers, a Jurassic Sounds Dinosaur Game ($20) with facts and T-Rex roars, and versions of Little Red Riding Hood and Hansel & Gretel, among many others. If you like the idea of sustainable, screen-free toys, the maker Qubs also made a clever wooden car STEM toy called Cody Block ($70) that introduces kids to basic coding concepts, and it’s on sale right now, down from $100.

articles.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
articles.text:
It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn’t all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro.
What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
Apple’s long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, an OLED iPad Mini, and more.
Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro
A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.
This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.
It’s also going to stick with the M5 series of chips for the time being — specifically, the M5 Pro and M5 Max. There might not be an M6 Pro or Max, even. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year.
M6 MacBook Pro
That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. It might also get a slight redesign, including a hole-punch style camera. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.
M6 iMac
The iMac is also expected to get an M6 update, nearly two years after its last revision. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model.
OLED iPad Mini
Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. The screen upgrade may add $100 to the cost, though. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

articles.title: GMO asks Japan for active cyber defence after hack
articles.text:
GMO Internet Group has asked Japan’s government to use its new active cyber defence powers against hackers who breached one of its services. The company made the request on Saturday, after the attackers demanded money.
In a stock exchange filing on Saturday, GMO said it wants state agencies to trace, block, and neutralise the attackers’ infrastructure. It said this would be the first use of the powers, which took effect on 1 October amid a wave of data leaks.
The breach hit Onamae.com Desktop Cloud. The service rents out Windows servers to traders who run automated foreign-exchange tools such as MT4 and MT5 around the clock.
Up to 26,739 servers may have been affected, GMO said in an earlier incident report. The intruders planted malicious software on some customers’ servers, which may have exposed the trading logins stored there. From 21 October, customers reported trades they did not make.
The attackers then demanded payment, according to GMO. They threatened to keep placing unauthorised orders through accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms in Japan and abroad. They also threatened to leak customer and company data and to launch a ransomware attack.
GMO said it will not pay, because payment would not guarantee the stolen data is deleted or stop its misuse. It has asked police to open a criminal investigation. GMO also warned that anything the attackers publish may be partly false.
GMO has also asked major exchanges and brokers to block access from the service and cut off all active sessions. On 22 October, OANDA Japan told customers that MT4 and MT5 logins used on the service may have been exposed, and briefly held withdrawals for a security check.
Under the new law, police and Japan’s Self-Defense Forces can break into attackers’ servers and disable them before damage spreads, Jiji Press reported. However, GMO is not among the critical infrastructure operators the law designates, according to Impress Watch.
Meanwhile, GMO will pay ¥5,000 (about $32) to every current customer of the service, whether or not they lost money. It will also cover realised losses from unauthorised trades, minus any refunds from brokers.
The service will not return. Customers can move to a separate cloud service free for six months, and GMO will publish details of the loss claims process by 6 November. The company said it cannot yet estimate the cost to its earnings.

articles.title: I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
articles.text:
It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook.
I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
Not that I believe for a second that Apple will actually make a 2-in-1 convertible.
I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
Not that I believe for a second that Apple will actually make a 2-in-1 convertible.
Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.
The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse.
The Yoga 9n’s included stylus works for note-taking and drawing on its excellent OLED display, but you can also use it on the haptic trackpad for a Wacom-like experience, without blocking the screen with your hand. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient
I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Lenovo’s stylus relies on USB-C charging, which is fine, but not as convenient as always having it charged and ready to go while attached to your laptop.
I don’t expect Apple to make a standard convertible laptop after all this time. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky.
My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. The HomeView’s lack of apps is perplexing. The iPhone Duo is a little messy. Current MacBooks are so great, it’s easy to forget the butterfly keyboard fiasco wasn’t all that long ago. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.
Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: Here's how to test a CR2032 battery to see if it's good - Engadget
articles.text:
Here's how to test a CR2032 battery to see if it's good
You won't need expensive equipment or invest much time.
Your car key fob suddenly needs several presses to unlock the door. Your AirTag stops responding when you try to locate it. Before blaming either gadget, it's worth checking the battery inside. One common type is the CR2032, a 3V lithium coin cell also used in Samsung's SmartTag2 and some smart home sensors. Depending on the device and how often it's used, one can last way over a year.
A multimeter can help you check the battery's voltage, and it's a good addition to your toolbox if you don't already own one. There are cheaper ways to check, too, but don't mistake a voltage reading for a complete picture of battery health.
How to test a CR2032 battery with a multimeter
Begin by checking the battery itself. If you spot crusty residue, rust-colored patches, swelling or leakage, skip the test and replace it. Have a look at the device's contacts too, since corrosion there can cause trouble even with a good battery.
Remove the CR2032 and set your digital multimeter to DC voltage (V with a solid line over a dashed line). Plug the black lead into COM and the red lead into the V or VΩ port. If your meter doesn't automatically select a range, set it above 3V, typically 20V.
Hold the battery by its edges over a nonconductive surface. Touch the red probe to the broad face marked with a plus sign (+) and the black probe to the center of the smaller negative face underneath. Keep the probe tips from touching each other or bridging the battery's terminals. A negative reading simply means you've reversed the probes.
A fresh CR2032 typically reads around 3V, while a reading closer to 2.5V is a good reason to bring in a replacement. But don't give that 3V reading too much credit though. A multimeter draws almost no current, so a battery might look fine on the display but struggle when your key fob or tracker actually needs power. There's no single pass-or-fail reading for every device. If it keeps acting up, try a fresh CR2032 unit before assuming the device is faulty.
No multimeter? Here's how to check your AirTag or key fob battery
A dedicated coin-cell tester is another option. Some cost around $10, although certain models only measure voltage rather than how the battery performs under load. Basic multimeters can cost less than $20 and are good for checking other batteries or troubleshooting low-voltage electronics. Still, buying either just to diagnose one suspect $3 battery is a harder sell.
There's also the LED trick, assuming you have one lying around. A small red or yellow LED is a better choice than a blue or white one because it generally needs less voltage to light up. Touch its longer leg to the CR2032's positive side and the shorter leg to the negative side. If it lights up, the battery can supply some current. That's about all it proves. The LED won't tell you how much life is left, and one that stays dark doesn't necessarily mean the battery is dead.
AirTag owners can check Find My before opening anything. Select Items inside the app and tap your AirTag. If it says "Low Battery," or shows a depleted battery icon, skip the testing and replace the CR2032. Some CR2032 batteries have bitterant coatings that may prevent proper contact, even when they're brand new. Apple recommends packaging marked "Compatible with Apple AirTag" when replacing an AirTag battery, and says an AirTag's battery lasts more than a year, while Samsung rates the SmartTag2 for up to 500 days in normal mode.
After removing a CR2032, keep it out of children's reach and tape its terminals before taking them to a battery collection facility. If one is swallowed, seek emergency medical care immediately, as serious internal injuries can occur in as little as two hours.

articles.title: What makes a fax HIPAA compliant when AI reads the page
articles.text:
HHS has never told healthcare to stop faxing. Its guidance says the Privacy Rule permits physicians to disclose PHI to another provider by fax for treatment, as long as reasonable and appropriate safeguards are in place.
Take two identical referral forms sent the same morning. One moves through an encrypted, logged channel covered by a signed business associate agreement (BAA), and OCR software indexes it into the chart. The other sits in an output tray in a shared hallway. Same document, same law, two very different compliance positions.
HIPAA regulates the safeguards around a fax
Does a fax need to be HIPAA compliant? For a covered entity or business associate sending protected health information, yes. But a fax machine, an app or a cloud service can’t be compliant on an organization’s behalf. The rule asks whether the organization has reasonable safeguards around each disclosure.
Covered entities, HHS says, “must have in place reasonable and appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards” for PHI sent by fax, such as confirming the recipient’s number and choosing to pre-program frequently used numbers. Once a faxed page becomes a digital file, the Security Rule’s safeguard standards apply as well.
“Most people start by asking whether a fax service is HIPAA compliant, and that’s the wrong place to start,” says Adam Korbl, Founder and CEO of iFax. “HIPAA doesn’t certify a fax machine or an app. I’d rather people ask who can open the document, whether anything done to it is logged, and whether the BAA covers the software reading the page, not just the line carrying it.”
Korbl’s questions all concern the workflow. A fax that arrives intact but sits in a shared queue, or gets filed to the wrong chart, can still expose a patient’s information, and the industry’s breach numbers are already high: The HIPAA Journal counted 772 large healthcare data breaches on the OCR portal for 2025 as of early January 2026, a record.
What a compliant fax workflow covers now
OCR engines, extraction models and routing rules all handle the page now, and each of those steps carries the same obligations as the transmission.
Encryption is the obvious place to begin. Under the current Security Rule it’s an “addressable” specification, a label The HIPAA Journal notes has led some covered entities to treat it as optional when it never was, and for cloud fax it should reach the OCR text as well as the stored images, at rest and in transit. Every send, receipt, view and routing decision should also leave an entry that someone can pull up later.
The BAA holds the arrangement together legally. HHS’s sample BAA provisions outline what the contract must require of a vendor, including Security Rule safeguards, breach reporting and matching terms for subcontractors. Under HHS cloud guidance, a cloud provider storing ePHI is a business associate even without the key, and the conduit exception “is limited to transmission-only services.” By that logic, a phone carrier moving the fax signal counts as a conduit, while a cloud fax platform storing copies generally counts as a business associate. If OCR or data extraction runs at a separate company, that company needs coverage too, usually under a subcontractor BAA with the vendor.
HHS’s advice on misdialed fax numbers applies to routing rules as well. If a rule misfires and files a referral under the wrong patient, the result is no different from a misdialed number. Staff should look over uncertain matches before anything gets filed.
Here a vendor can do a lot of the work. iFax says its healthcare platform pairs AES-256 encryption in transit and at rest with signed BAAs, role-based access and audit logs, and runs OCR inside the same controlled infrastructure. That handles the technical side. Policies, staff training and the risk analysis are still the covered entities to manage.
Access control rounds out the list, and skipping it has a documented cost. The 2024 Change Healthcare attack began with compromised credentials on a system where MFA wasn’t turned on, and it ultimately affected approximately 193 million individuals.
The security rule is catching up with software that reads
HHS has started writing AI into the rules, though the biggest changes are still proposals. The Security Rule overhaul published on January 6, 2025 would make encryption of ePHI mandatory with limited exceptions, require multi-factor authentication and call for an annual technology asset inventory and network map. It also names AI directly: a risk analysis “must include consideration of, among other things, the type and amount of ePHI accessed by the AI tool, to whom the data is disclosed, and to whom the output is provided.”
Timing is uncertain: after nearly 5,000 comments, final action is now targeted for July 2027. OCR’s own estimate put first-year compliance costs at $9 billion, and the proposal would give organizations 240 days after the final rule to comply. None of that is likely to change who does what, though: vendors provide the tools, and practices still run the program.
“We can give a practice the encryption, the audit trail and a controlled place for OCR to run. The policies, the staff training, the risk analysis, that’s for the practice’s to own, not ours.” Korbl says.
That division gets blurry when staff bring in AI tools on their own. In an Imprivata-commissioned survey of 250 health security and AI leaders, 72% said AI tools or agents are being deployed without formal IT approval, Axios reported. Tools that IT never approved are unlikely to appear in an asset inventory, let alone be checked against a BAA, and an inventory requirement like the one HHS proposed is meant to surface them. The survey also found that 28% of organizations have agentic AI in production already, while 44% are piloting or testing it.
Buy the stack, run the program
A practice can buy a compliant document stack. Compliance isn’t sold that way. It has to be run from inside the practice, with written policies that get updated and staff who are trained on them. A fax vendor that can’t produce encryption, access controls, audit logs and a signed BAA shouldn’t make the shortlist. For the AI layer, buyers should push further and find out where the reading actually happens, whether the BAA extends that far, whether automated actions are logged and who checks the matches the software isn’t sure about.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 24/10: Thế giới tăng mạnh, xăng trong nước có kỳ giảm sâu
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này (23/10) tăng mạnh. Giá dầu Brent lên mức gần 117 USD/thùng, mức cao nhất trong gần 6 tháng.
Ở phiên giao dịch 23/10, theo dữ liệu từ Oilprice, giá dầu Brent chốt phiên ở mức 116,7 USD/thùng, tăng 3,14% so với phiên liền trước. Đây là mức chốt phiên cao nhất kể từ ngày 29/4. 
Còn giá dầu WTI đóng cửa phiên 23/10 ở mức 103,3 USD/thùng, tăng 3,82% so với phiên liền trước.
Tính chung trong cả tuần này, giá dầu Brent tăng 6%, trong khi giá dầu WTI tăng 2,3%.
Giá dầu thế giới tăng mạnh trong phiên cuối tuần khi các cuộc tấn công của lực lượng Houthi nhằm vào Saudi Arabia và sự cố tràn dầu ngoài khơi tại Các Tiểu Vương quốc Ảrập Thống nhất (UAE) làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguồn cung năng lượng.
Reuters đưa tin, ngày 22/10, tập đoàn dầu khí Saudi Aramco đã yêu cầu sơ tán nhân viên tại trụ sở chính ở Dhahran, thành phố nằm gần Vịnh Ba Tư và Bahrain, trong bối cảnh giao tranh giữa Saudi Arabia và lực lượng Houthi tại Yemen leo thang.
Các cuộc đụng độ giữa lực lượng Houthi (do Iran hậu thuẫn) và liên minh do Saudi Arabia dẫn đầu đã diễn ra dữ dội kể từ khi lực lượng Houthi tiến về Bab el-Mandeb, một điểm nghẽn giao thông hàng hải ở cửa Biển Đỏ.
Trong khi đó, cơ quan chức năng của UAE cũng thông báo phát hiện một vụ tràn dầu.
Ngày 23/10, Bộ Biến đổi Khí hậu và Môi trường UAE thông báo phát hiện dầu tràn từ một tàu chở dầu ngoài khơi, gây ảnh hưởng đến các bãi biển thuộc tiểu vương quốc Umm Al Quwain, phía bắc Dubai. Song cơ quan này không nêu nguyên nhân xảy ra sự cố và các cơ quan chức năng chưa xác định được tàu chở dầu liên quan.
Sự cố xảy ra trong bối cảnh các vụ tấn công nhằm vào tàu thuyền gia tăng trong những tuần gần đây tại vùng biển gần eo biển Hormuz, tuyến hàng hải quan trọng, nơi trung chuyển khoảng 1/5 sản lượng dầu toàn cầu trước khi xung đột giữa Iran và Mỹ nổ ra hồi cuối tháng 2 vừa qua.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (24/10) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 22/10, giá xăng dầu được điều chỉnh theo hướng xăng giảm, dầu diesel và mazut đều tăng so với kỳ điều hành liền trước.
Cụ thể, giá xăng E5RON92 giảm 1.610 đồng/lít so với kỳ trước, giá bán lẻ không cao hơn 25.361 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá xăng E10RON95-III hạ 1.816 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 25.213 đồng/lít.
Trái lại, giá dầu diesel 0.05S tăng 444 đồng/lít, lên mức tối đa 29.550 đồng/lít.
Giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 1.238 đồng/kg, giá bán không cao hơn 23.373 đồng/kg.
Dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương cho thấy, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera
articles.text:
Lee Chang Dong’s seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff – 2,600 employees – after which many died by suicide. Possible Love is the latest in a long line of Lee movies that engage with themes of class or labor or religion or compressed modernity, that uniquely Korean affliction, without feeling didactic.
Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera
In Possible Love, the director of Burning tackles labor struggle, human connection, and the nature of capturing others on film.
A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle. Possible Love picks up with the characters in the aftermath, a murkier time that defies easy understanding. The film opens with an epigraph: “Thou shall not covet.” What follows is a movie about characters who covet. They covet each other’s job, designer clothes, spouses, and positionality. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) is the long-suffering wife of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), her laid-off husband. At a funeral of a colleague who died by suicide, Mi-ok and Ho-seok meet another couple, documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her rich husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). And off we go.
The Verge spoke with Lee during his trip to New York about how he arrived at his politics, porousness between people, the properties of the camera, and what it is like to work with Netflix. The interview was conducted in Korean and translated into English.
I am also from Daegu. I wonder how this fact shaped you? And more broadly, to whom or what do you owe your political education?
As you know well, Daegu is referred to as the heartland of conservatism in Korea. I went to school there, all the way through university, so I grew up steeped in that conservative disposition and was influenced by it. But until I graduated from college, in the spring of 1980, I didn’t realize how politically conservative Daegu citizens were.
That spring, in May of 1980, I participated in protests against the Chun Doo-hwan regime as a university student. It was on the streets that I met them, the citizens, and experienced their hardline sentiments in a visceral way. It was shocking to me. Afterwards, I thought a lot about how come the people in Daegu were so politically conservative. In light of all that, the thoughts of a person I perceive as myself, that person’s attitude towards the world, could only be bound with a certain kind of tension.
I was interested in how different directors respond to similar social forces in different ways – like Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite and Park Chan Wook’s No Other Choice. I imagine you know them both personally. What is the conversation between you all when working on your various projects?
We do know each other personally, but we seldom talk about our work. It might be the result of coincidence. Though of course, there might be a certain inevitability hidden within them. We lived through the same modern Korean history, and you cannot call that coincidence.
One thing does come to mind. A long time ago, I think before he made Mother, Bong Joon Ho told me over drinks that he had almost finished writing a script and wanted to show it to me. It was a story about a mother, and he was wrestling with how he could portray that person’s pain, whether he even had the right to. He said he wanted to show me the script. But once he sobered up, maybe he forgot, because he never showed it to me. Later, when I saw the film, I felt I might understand what he had been talking about.
Possible Love is concerned with similar questions: How can I portray another person’s story, another person’s pain? What position am I in? How much distance should I keep from them? You could say that these questions around the ethics of the camera are connected to the worry Bong Joon Ho had back then.
Like Ye-ji, I come from the so-called margins, and now report on that terrain, which is perhaps why watching her character pursue a near-vampiric level of access, I felt something close to repulsion. How were you able to represent the filmmaker–participant dynamic so accurately?
I can’t say how accurate it is. I don’t think Ye-ji’s attitude can be generalized. Not every documentary filmmaker has a rich husband. Nevertheless you can say Ye-Ji captures something universal about filmmakers, or those who deal in other people’s stories, directors such as myself, or reporters, in that they aren’t exactly the people they portray. Even if they came from a lower class, they are no longer of it. Their position in life has changed. And yet, in order to do their work, what do they do? When someone else’s suffering unfolds dramatically in front of them, are they to capture the moment on tape, or should they step away from the camera? Or maybe it isn’t unfolding dramatically in front of them, in which case, do they create a certain effect by producing the moment, by staging it?
I think those are basically properties of the camera. The moment you hold a camera you have power, and the camera operates according to that power.
It’s not so much that I portrayed it so precisely, but these properties of the camera are something worth thinking through together.
For us filmmakers, we don’t belong to the world of our subjects, nor are we on the side of capital either. We are in the middle where we are, it can be said, in a neutral, or perhaps cowardly position. Despite that, those who make movies, those who tell stories of others, in the end, can, through their efforts, bring about some small change.
In this film, Ho-seok ends up pouring out what’s inside of him in front of the camera, which functions as a kind of treatment, even if that isn’t what Ye-ji intended.
Possible Love is a collaboration between you and screenwriter Oh Jung-mi. How did you two come to work together, and what does that collaboration look like?
She is a student I met at Korea National University of Arts. You could say it’s a school that draws the most talented and ambitious students, and she was special even among them. By special I mean she was creative and wrote well, of course, but she also has a perspective, and the ability to take a step back and regard something, and find meaning in things.
As I get older, I grow duller and numb, and set in my ways, and she is a friend who reliably jolts me out of it, which is very precious to me.
I think I’m lucky. Not just with Oh Jung-mi but everyone around me that I work with is very precious to me, and I feel lucky to have met them.
The problem with Oh Jung-mi, though, is that while working together, I kept scrapping projects. So she suffered. But she never left. She stayed beside me, and even though she herself is someone who makes and develops films, she has given me a lot of help up to now.
Ye-ji documents in service of higher purpose. Mi-ok’s character snaps photos of the table spread for no purpose at all. The footage from the helicopter captures a moment of police brutality. How does the function of cinema compare to all the other instances in which we hit record?
Ye-ji has a desire to capture in her camera vanishing laborers [and] the value of their labor — not unlike her dry cleaner father. And yet, it is undeniable that she also regards their lives as source material for her own movie. As narrative filmmakers, stories of others in pain often is nothing but material for a commercial movie.
As for Mi-ok, she knows about the properties of the camera, but she, too, has a desire: to broadcast her pain, and her problems. She has a secondary desire, which is that she wonders if her husband’s traumas may not be healed through the camera, because she believes that his biggest issue is keeping all his problems, his despair and his anger, hidden.
So each has their own desires regarding the camera.
As a filmmaker, firstly, I had the goal of conveying the contents of the documentary Ye-ji was making, of capturing the sufferings of the laid-off laborers. I believed what Ye-ji tried to show, I had to show through my own film.
The group therapy session scene, for example, could be very long and tedious, and for some viewers it might be something that they cannot emotionally relate to, because they came to see a narrative film, not documentary. Despite that, I felt I had to convey it.
Regarding the crackdown scene, some of it appears through archival footage shot from a distance. But as someone making a fiction film, I also have a responsibility to convey Ho-seok’s subjective memory cinematically. So you could say within the narrative structure of Ye-ji’s documentary, multiple layers of roles and goals co-exist.
What are some notes you received from your American movie executives that felt unique to working in the American system versus Korean?
I didn’t feel that at all. From pre-production through post-production, Netflix, as the investor, never once interfered or offered unsolicited notes. Of course, I can’t generalize from that. I haven’t asked everyone else. But I had none of that. In that sense they absolutely guaranteed my independence and freedom as a director.
Now the film is finished and we are promoting it, and in particular part of what we call the Oscar campaign. I probably wouldn’t have gotten this kind of help without Netflix, that’s clear.
Possible Love was released in select US theaters October 23rd and will be available on Netflix globally on November 6th.

articles.title: The beneficial purpose of 'IQ' on your Anker chargers - Engadget
articles.text:
The beneficial purpose of 'IQ' on your Anker chargers
Anker's PowerIQ technology helps identify and charge your devices more efficiently.
Cutting through marketing slogans and tech jargon can feel like a full-time job when you're shopping for gadgets, but it's worth knowing exactly what you're getting with your new electronics. That's especially true of chargers and batteries, where making the wrong choice can leave you without power when you need it or even damage your devices. The PowerIQ label has appeared on Anker chargers for years now, and it's actually worth knowing what it means before picking one up.
Chargers and electronics use multiple different charging standards for delivering and receiving power. You may have seen other terms like QC (Quick Charge) or PD (Power Delivery), depending on which manufacturer's products you're using. PowerIQ, or PIQ, is Anker's proprietary tech that governs how quickly chargers with the technology send power to a connected device's battery.
Charging standards aren't the whole picture for charging speed
According to Anker, PowerIQ chargers are able to detect what device they're connected to and adjust their power output based on what voltage is best for the connected battery. In theory, that allows PowerIQ chargers to charge devices quickly without delivering too much power and damaging the connected device. PowerIQ chargers are generally considered safe for that reason. Fast-charging devices always carries some risk of diminishing their battery life in the long term, and while PowerIQ chargers might offset that risk somewhat, there's no way of eliminating it completely.
PowerIQ chargers aren't necessarily any faster than those using other standards. Charging speed is determined by the device being charged as much as by the charger, so pure power output doesn't mean as much as it might seem. If a device can only accept a 12W charging speed, for instance, it doesn't matter if a charger can deliver 100W, which some current chargers using any standard are capable of.
Not every device is designed to accept every standard, either. PD is the most common standard, but QC is widely used in Android devices as well. These days, the distinctions matter less than they used to, since the latest versions of PD and QC (4.0) are partially cross-compatible with each other. The same is true of PowerIQ. The latest version of PowerIQ, PIQ 4.0, is compatible with QC and PD 3.0, meaning newer PIQ chargers support fast-charging on essentially any device.
Newer Anker chargers let you see what PowerIQ is doing
New Anker chargers have also integrated displays that let you see information about the devices you're charging. Since PowerIQ chargers monitor the devices they're connected to, these chargers can display information about temperature and wattage in real time. Whether that information is actually useful to have is another matter, but there's certainly no harm in being able to see it at a glance if you're interested.

articles.title: Meta Finally Ditched the Cameras—and Made Its Best Smart Glasses Yet
articles.text:
I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.
“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”
The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.
It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)
It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)
