articles.title: Bỏ nghề viễn thông, vợ chồng 9X nuôi gần 40.000 con gà, lãi 1 tỷ đồng/năm
articles.text:
Bỏ nghề cũ, đầu tư hàng tỷ đồng nuôi gà đẻ trứng
Tại thôn Xuân Sơn, xã Toàn Lưu, Hà Tĩnh, trang trại rộng gần 1ha của vợ chồng anh Nguyễn Hữu Dũng (SN 1995) được đầu tư theo mô hình chuồng nuôi kín. Bên trong các dãy chuồng, đàn gà được nuôi theo từng lứa, cung cấp hàng chục nghìn quả trứng mỗi ngày.
Tốt nghiệp ngành Điện tử viễn thông, anh Dũng từng làm việc trong lĩnh vực viễn thông trước khi chuyển hướng sang chăn nuôi. Vợ anh, chị Đặng Thị Oanh (SN 1996), tốt nghiệp ngành Thú y, Trường Đại học Nông Lâm Huế, phụ trách kỹ thuật và chăm sóc sức khỏe đàn gà.
Ý tưởng xây dựng trang trại xuất phát từ hoạt động kinh doanh của gia đình. Bố mẹ anh Dũng làm nghề bán tạp hóa, trong đó có kinh doanh trứng gà. Qua tìm hiểu thị trường, anh nhận thấy một phần nguồn trứng cung cấp cho địa phương được vận chuyển từ các tỉnh phía Bắc vào. Từ đó, hai vợ chồng bắt đầu tìm hiểu mô hình chăn nuôi nhằm chủ động nguồn cung tại chỗ.
Sau thời gian tìm hiểu, anh Dũng đến các tỉnh phía Bắc học hỏi kinh nghiệm nuôi gà chuyên trứng. Cuối năm 2022, anh quyết định mua lại khu đất gần 1ha tại xã Toàn Lưu và đầu tư xây dựng trang trại, ban đầu nuôi khoảng 7.000 con.
Theo anh Dũng, tổng vốn đầu tư ban đầu khoảng 6-7 tỷ đồng, bao gồm tiền đất, xây dựng chuồng trại và mua con giống. Do chưa có nhiều kinh nghiệm thực tế, hai vợ chồng lựa chọn cách phát triển từng bước, vừa chăn nuôi vừa hoàn thiện kỹ thuật và tìm kiếm đầu ra. Từ quy mô ban đầu, trang trại dần được mở rộng lên gần 40.000 con.
Hiện trang trại có 4 chuồng, mỗi chuồng rộng hơn 1.000m², sử dụng hệ thống nuôi kín với các dãy lồng. Cơ sở có 4 lao động làm việc thường xuyên, phụ trách chăm sóc đàn gà, vệ sinh chuồng trại và thu gom trứng.
Mỗi ngày cung cấp khoảng 35.000 quả trứng
Theo anh Dũng, giống gà Ai Cập trắng chuyên trứng được gia đình lựa chọn có năng suất tiềm năng khoảng 330 quả/con/năm trong điều kiện chăm sóc phù hợp.
Gà giống một ngày tuổi có giá khoảng 30.000 đồng/con. Trang trại nhập khoảng 11.000 con mỗi đợt để nuôi theo từng lứa. Gà bắt đầu đẻ khi đạt khoảng 17-20 tuần tuổi và được khai thác trong khoảng một năm trước khi thay đàn.
Khi đàn gà bước vào giai đoạn đẻ ổn định, trang trại thu được khoảng 35.000 quả trứng mỗi ngày. Trứng được thu gom, phân loại và đưa đi tiêu thụ trong ngày, chủ yếu thông qua các đầu mối tại Hà Tĩnh và những tỉnh lân cận.
Anh Dũng cho biết, ở giai đoạn đầu, hai vợ chồng gặp khó khăn trong việc tìm kiếm khách hàng và xây dựng mạng lưới tiêu thụ. Khi quy mô đàn gà và sản lượng trứng tăng lên, việc duy trì đầu ra ổn định càng trở nên quan trọng, bởi trứng là sản phẩm cần được tiêu thụ thường xuyên.
Không chỉ trứng thương phẩm, đầu ra cho đàn gà sau chu kỳ khai thác cũng là vấn đề cần tính toán. Anh Dũng cho hay mỗi năm trang trại có khoảng 30 tấn gà thải loại cần tiêu thụ. Gia đình tìm các mối thu mua để đưa số gà này ra thị trường phục vụ chế biến thực phẩm, trong đó có sản phẩm gà ủ muối.
Để hạn chế tác động của thời tiết và giảm nguy cơ dịch bệnh, trang trại sử dụng hệ thống chuồng kín, quạt thông gió và dàn làm mát. Theo anh Dũng, nhiệt độ trong chuồng được duy trì ở mức khoảng 28-29 độ C, tùy điều kiện thời tiết và giai đoạn phát triển của đàn gà.
Đàn gà được tiêm vaccine định kỳ, song vẫn có thể mắc các bệnh về đường tiêu hóa, hô hấp hoặc sinh sản. Anh Dũng ước tính tỷ lệ hao hụt của đàn gà khoảng 7-10% mỗi năm.
Bên cạnh đó, chất lượng thức ăn cũng được gia đình quan tâm nhằm duy trì sức khỏe đàn gà và năng suất trứng. Theo anh Dũng, trang trại lựa chọn loại cám phù hợp, trong đó ngô chiếm khoảng 70% thành phần theo công thức phối trộn mà anh sử dụng.
Phân gà được thu gom, ủ vi sinh rồi bán cho người dân địa phương sử dụng làm phân bón. Cách xử lý này vừa tạo thêm nguồn thu, vừa góp phần hạn chế lượng chất thải phát sinh trong quá trình chăn nuôi.
Theo anh Dũng, doanh thu của trang trại ước đạt 8-10 tỷ đồng/năm, lợi nhuận khoảng 1 tỷ đồng sau khi trừ chi phí. Đây là mức ước tính của gia đình và có thể thay đổi theo giá trứng, giá thức ăn, năng suất đàn gà cũng như chi phí phòng dịch, thay đàn.
Thời gian tới, hai vợ chồng dự kiến đầu tư thêm hệ thống cho ăn, uống tự động nhằm giảm công việc thủ công và nâng cao hiệu quả quản lý. Theo anh Dũng, bên cạnh vốn đầu tư ban đầu, khả năng kiểm soát chi phí thức ăn, duy trì năng suất, chủ động phòng dịch và bảo đảm đầu ra sẽ quyết định hiệu quả lâu dài của mô hình.
Trao đổi với PV VietNamNet, lãnh đạo UBND xã Toàn Lưu đánh giá mô hình nuôi gà đẻ trứng của anh Dũng là một trong những mô hình phát triển kinh tế hiệu quả tại địa phương. “Việc áp dụng tiến bộ khoa học kỹ thuật vào chăm sóc đàn gà giúp mô hình mang lại thu nhập cho gia đình, đồng thời góp phần thúc đẩy phát triển kinh tế chăn nuôi tại địa phương”, vị lãnh đạo nói.

articles.title: Laika has spent 20 years building up to Wildwood
articles.text:
Across several decades in Hollywood, Caleb Deschanel has seen a lot. He served as cinematographer on films like The Passion of the Christ and The Patriot, worked on sequences in The Godfather and Titanic, and directed a few episodes of Twin Peaks. Even still, nothing could quite prepare him for his first stop-motion project: working as the cinematographer on Wildwood, the latest release from Coraline studio Laika. While he knew that stop-motion was a long and involved process, he was still surprised by just how much work went into these movies. “When I started I thought it was one thing, and then I quickly found out that it was another thing,” Deschanel says. “It was much more complicated than I expected.”
Laika has spent 20 years building up to Wildwood
How the stop-motion animation studio blends traditional techniques with modern tech.
Laika has spent 20 years building up to Wildwood
How the stop-motion animation studio blends traditional techniques with modern tech.
Wildwood has been a long time coming. Laika CEO Travis Knight originally optioned the rights for the book of the same name, written by Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy, in 2011. But production didn’t begin until a decade later. “I’ve been working on it in some form or another for 16 years,” Knight, who also directed Wildwood, says. “The reason why I stuck with it, the reason why I had to make this movie no matter what, is because of what it meant to me personally. Underneath it all, it’s a story about love and loss and grief, it’s about the impossible things that love asks of us, and that meant something to me personally in a very profound way.”
It’s also the biggest production Laika has ever undertaken. Wildwood tells the story of a young girl named Prue who has to venture into the “impassable wilderness” that surrounds Portland in order to find her baby brother. When she enters the forest she discovers a fantasy realm reminiscent of Narnia, with magical spells, talking animals, and warring factions. It required nearly 50 animators and more than 200 puppets to pull it off, and the film is full of ambitious sequences, like a 12-minute battle with dozens of soldiers and a chase scene through a bustling Portland, where Prue’s brother is carried away by a gigantic murder of crows.
According to head of animation Brad Schiff, the studio’s ethos involves mixing “old-school craft with modern technology.” With each project, he says, Laika develops new techniques. If something works well, they then push the idea even further on the next project. For instance, on Laika’s previous film, Missing Link, the main character was outfitted with a diaphragm so that when an animator turned a screw on the puppet’s back, the diaphragm could expand or contract, creating the illusion that it was breathing. This has since become the standard for puppets in Laika’s films.
These may sound like small details, but over the years they add up. For costume designer Deb Cook, there wasn’t a single innovation on Wildwood that stood out to her, but rather the sheer number of tools she had at her disposal. “Over time we’ve gathered together a library of techniques that we’ve been able to put into practice on this movie,” she says. This was especially important on Wildwood, which features a huge range of costumes; in the city sequences everyone is dressed in modern clothing, whereas in the forest characters have more fantastical looks.
“It was much more complicated than I expected.”
For Wildwood, many of the advancements came down to materials. The costumes made use of more flexible fabrics, for example, and the team also engineered a new process for creating silicone that’s lighter and more durable than what they previously used. “We’ve done this so we can wean ourselves off of foam latex, which is stinky and it shrinks over time, and five years later it kind of just crumbles,” says Oliver Jones, head of characters and practical effects. “There are advantages to rethinking a lot of these materials that were our go-to probably since King Kong.”
The scale of Wildwood has also forced the studio to adopt another seemingly much more boring practice: being better organized. “They’ve been misplaced,” Cook says, when asked if she’s ever lost a puppet. “There’s now a very sophisticated tracking system because there are so many moving parts, and so many stages around the studio.”
And while much has been said about the large and elaborate sequences in the film — Knight says the epic battle scene is “probably the most technically challenging thing that we’ve ever done” — all of these techniques are designed to imbue more humanity into characters that are portrayed by puppets. In that regard, small details like the flow of fabric or the impression of breathing are vitally important.
“We also have really subtle and intimate scenes, quiet scenes that don’t have a lot of flash, that have virtually no sound design or music, where the only thing that you’re experiencing is the grief of a father talking about a secret that he’s been holding on to for 15 years, or a quiet moment of a woman grieving the loss of her son,” Knight explains. “These are moments where you have nowhere to hide and the performances of these little puppets — these little assemblages of steel and silicon and fabric that have no life of their own — completely spring to life because of the hand and the artistry of the human behind it. Those are the moments that I’m most proud of.”
In this way, the long road to Wildwood hitting theaters makes a lot of sense. Laika has been around for just over 20 years, and over the course of each film the studio has innovated to steadily push its craft forward. Knight may have been thinking about the film for 16 years, but creating the version that is coming out in 2026 wouldn’t have been possible without all of the learnings spread across films like ParaNorman and Kubo and the Two Strings.
For Knight, it’s been especially gratifying to bring it to life with a team of both Laika veterans and newcomers, including not only Deschanel but also a handful of young animators for whom Wildwood was their first feature film project. Some were young enough that Coraline, Laika’s very first film, was what inspired them to get into the field in the first place. “I was really moved by that,” says Knight. “It also made me feel old as shit.”
Wildwood is in theaters now.

articles.title: How to improve your PC's airflow for better cooling - Engadget
articles.text:
How to improve your PC's airflow for better cooling
Here's how to think about your fans.
When you're building or upgrading a PC, chances are you're thinking more about how to improve your machine's performance than you are about where you're going to put the fans. Improving airflow might not be as exciting as adding a new graphics card, but it's essential to getting the most out of your rig. Fortunately, there are a few simple principles you can apply to any PC build to keep all your components running cool.
It's important to understand exactly what you're trying to accomplish when improving your PC's airflow. PC components generate heat as they run, which gets trapped in the case, degrading system performance if things get too hot. The point of fans is to draw cooler air from outside the case over those components and exhaust the hot air they generate outside. That means the first step should be placing your PC somewhere that already has decent airflow — not in a corner of the room, not shoved under your desk, and definitely not crowded in with other electronics.
Fan placement and pressure are the keys to good airflow
Where you place your fans matters even more. Since hot air naturally rises and the hottest components in your case (the CPU and GPU) tend to be near the back, it's best to pull cool air from the front and bottom and exhaust hot air out the top and back. Not every system needs fans on the top and bottom, but adding them is a good first step if you're struggling to keep your PC cool with just the front and back fans.
In addition to improving airflow, fans change the air pressure within your case. If the air pressure inside a case is higher than the air pressure outside (called positive pressure), air will naturally try to escape through any gaps it can. If case pressure is lower, it will instead draw air in through those gaps, bringing dust along with it. Completely optimized airflow will maintain neutral pressure, where cool air enters the case at the same rate that hot air exits. Precisely neutral pressure can be hard to achieve, though, so it's usually best to aim for slightly positive pressure by ensuring that your case is drawing in a little more air than it's exhausting to avoid drawing in excess dust.
If you're buying new fans, pay attention to their size and speed. The standard case fan size is 120mm, and anything larger than that will pull in more air but at a lower pressure. That's important when considering that intake fans at the front and bottom of a case are usually pulling air through a mesh screen, which further reduces the pressure of the air coming in. Because of that, it's usually better to run intake fans at a higher speed to increase their pressure if you have the option. Also keep in mind that larger fans are usually quieter than smaller ones, so they tend to be a better choice if noise is a concern. There's no precise formula for optimal fan size and speed, so you may have to experiment with your setup to find what works for you.
How to keep any PC running cool
Fans are by far the most important part of improving your PC's airflow, but there are ways to help them do their job. The easiest and most obvious is to regularly open your case and clean out dust using pressurized air. Placing dust filters on open gaps in the case can also keep dust from building up, but it's important to remember to clean them regularly as well.
Purchasing a new case built for optimal airflow is also an option, but you can achieve good airflow in just about any case. Just avoid any cases that have a solid front panel and instead opt for one with a mesh panel in front of the intake fans. Practicing good cable management is important no matter what case you have. Remember that the goal is to ensure air can flow as freely as possible from the front of the case to the back and arrange your case accordingly.

articles.title: 9 địa phương phải tăng trưởng trên 15%: Gỡ điểm nghẽn để tăng tốc
articles.text:
Theo Bộ Tài chính, lũy kế đến hết ngày 8/10/2026, giải ngân vốn đầu tư công nguồn ngân sách nhà nước đạt 652 nghìn tỷ đồng, bằng 63,8% kế hoạch Thủ tướng Chính phủ giao.
Quý IV đầy áp lực: 9 địa phương phải tăng trưởng trên 15%
Bà Nguyễn Thị Mai Hạnh, Trưởng ban Hệ thống Tài khoản quốc gia, Cục Thống kê (Bộ Tài chính) cho biết, tăng trưởng kinh tế 9 tháng năm 2026 được hỗ trợ bởi ba động lực chính: đầu tư công tạo thêm khối lượng sản xuất; công nghiệp và xuất khẩu mở rộng đầu ra; tiêu dùng trong nước duy trì nhịp tăng của thương mại, dịch vụ.
Các động lực tăng trưởng mới như khoa học - công nghệ, đổi mới sáng tạo và kinh tế số đang được thúc đẩy mạnh mẽ hơn, từng bước thâm nhập vào các ngành công nghiệp và dịch vụ có hàm lượng công nghệ cao. Tuy nhiên, ở giai đoạn hiện nay, các động lực này chủ yếu đóng vai trò hỗ trợ, chưa thực sự trở thành lực kéo chính cho tăng trưởng.
Quốc hội đặt mục tiêu GDP năm 2026 phấn đấu tăng từ 10% trở lên. Trên cơ sở kết quả 9 tháng tăng 9,01%, để đạt mục tiêu tăng trưởng cả năm, GDP quý IV cần tăng khoảng 12,5% (cao hơn khoảng 4,1 điểm phần trăm so quý IV/2025). Theo bà Hạnh, mục tiêu này được xem là khó khăn và rất áp lực.
Ngày 3/10/2026, Chính phủ ban hành Nghị quyết số 312/NQ-CP về phiên họp thường kỳ tháng 9 và Hội nghị trực tuyến Chính phủ với địa phương, kèm phụ lục kịch bản tăng trưởng quý IV của các ngành, lĩnh vực và địa phương.
Chỉ tiêu tăng trưởng quý IV/2026 của 9 địa phương được Chính phủ giao tại Nghị quyết số 312.
Theo kịch bản này, 9 địa phương được yêu cầu tăng trưởng trên 15% trong quý IV. Trong đó, Lạng Sơn có yêu cầu tăng trưởng cao nhất là 18,41%, bởi sau 9 tháng mới tăng 7,52% trong khi mục tiêu cả năm là 10,61%.
Tiếp theo là Vĩnh Long 17,25%, Thanh Hóa 17,10%, Cà Mau 16,70%, Quảng Trị 16,64%, Hà Nội 16,55%, Cần Thơ 16,08%, Hải Phòng 15,39% và Tuyên Quang 15,04%.
12 địa phương được giao mức tăng trưởng từ 13% đến dưới 15%, đó là: An Giang 14,95%, Cao Bằng 14,86%, Nghệ An 14,51%, Bắc Ninh 14,37%, Quảng Ninh 14,24%, Điện Biên 13,97%, Sơn La 13,85%, Huế 13,72%, Đắk Lắk 13,62%, Đà Nẵng 13,61%, Phú Thọ 13,50% và TPHCM 13,23%.
6 địa phương yêu cầu tăng trưởng dưới 13% là: Lâm Đồng 12,87%, Lào Cai 12,66%, Hưng Yên 12,14%, Gia Lai 11,33%, Lai Châu 11,16% và Đồng Tháp 10,36%.
Địa phương cần phản ứng nhanh, gỡ điểm nghẽn
Với những địa phương yêu cầu tăng trưởng cao, chẳng hạn như Lạng Sơn, làm sao để đạt 18,41% trong giai đoạn “nước rút” cuối năm?
Chia sẻ với PV VietNamNet, TS Nguyễn Minh Thảo, Trưởng ban Nghiên cứu Môi trường kinh doanh và Năng lực cạnh tranh, Viện Nghiên cứu quản lý kinh tế Trung ương (CIEM) cho rằng, để hoàn thành mục tiêu tăng trưởng 10% trong năm 2026, các địa phương cần bám sát kịch bản tăng trưởng đã xây dựng, đồng thời tập trung khai thác các động lực có khả năng tạo sức bật trong những tháng cuối năm.
Theo bà Thảo, dựa trên cơ cấu ngành kinh tế và tiềm năng của từng địa phương, Chính phủ đã giao chỉ tiêu tăng trưởng cho các tỉnh, thành ngay từ đầu năm. Trong đó, chú trọng các địa phương có đóng góp lớn vào GDP cả nước, bởi có năm chỉ 5-6 tỉnh, thành phố trực thuộc Trung ương đã chiếm khoảng 50% GDP. Đây là những địa phương cần tăng tốc để tạo lực kéo cho tăng trưởng chung.
Trước hết, mỗi địa phương phải rà soát khoảng cách giữa kết quả thực hiện và mục tiêu được giao, từ đó xác định rõ những ngành, lĩnh vực cần tăng tốc trong thời gian còn lại của năm.
Bà Thảo nhận định, đầu tư công tiếp tục là một trong những động lực quan trọng. Các địa phương cần đẩy nhanh tiến độ triển khai và giải ngân vốn đầu tư công.
Bên cạnh đó, tận dụng xu hướng tiêu dùng tăng vào dịp cuối năm và chuẩn bị Tết để thúc đẩy tổng mức bán lẻ hàng hóa, doanh thu dịch vụ tiêu dùng, qua đó tăng đóng góp của khu vực tiêu dùng và dịch vụ vào tăng trưởng kinh tế.
Xuất khẩu cũng là động lực cần được khai thác mạnh hơn. Nhu cầu tại một số thị trường xuất khẩu thường tăng vào cuối năm, tạo cơ hội để các địa phương và doanh nghiệp đẩy mạnh hoạt động xuất khẩu, đóng góp vào mục tiêu tăng trưởng chung.
Một nguồn lực khác cần được khơi thông là đầu tư tư nhân. Theo bà Thảo, dù thời gian còn lại của năm không nhiều để tạo ra sự bứt phá, việc tháo gỡ khó khăn cho hoạt động đầu tư, kinh doanh vẫn rất cần thiết. Đầu tư công không chỉ trực tiếp đóng góp vào tăng trưởng mà còn có thể tạo đà, thu hút thêm nguồn lực từ khu vực tư nhân.
Để các giải pháp phát huy hiệu quả, các địa phương cần theo dõi sát tiến độ thực hiện mục tiêu, thậm chí kiểm tra theo tuần thay vì chỉ đánh giá theo tháng. Những vướng mắc về giải phóng mặt bằng, nguồn cung vật liệu, giá cả và các biến động từ bên ngoài cần được xử lý kịp thời.
Trước những thay đổi bất lợi của thị trường quốc tế, chẳng hạn biến động giá xăng dầu, nguyên liệu, địa phương cần có cơ chế phản ứng nhanh để duy trì hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh, hạn chế gián đoạn và tạo điều kiện để tăng trưởng bứt phá.
Không chờ đến cuối năm mới tăng tốc
Để tăng trưởng bền vững, TS Nguyễn Minh Thảo cho rằng bài học quan trọng từ thực tiễn giải ngân đầu tư công là phải triển khai nhiệm vụ ngay từ đầu năm, thay vì chờ đến khi kết quả không đạt kỳ vọng mới tăng tốc vào cuối năm.
Việc giao chỉ tiêu tăng trưởng cần đi kèm các kịch bản có tính khả thi, được xây dựng trên cơ sở đánh giá đúng năng lực và nguồn lực của từng địa phương. Đồng thời, các kịch bản này cần được rà soát thường xuyên để điều chỉnh khi cần thiết, tránh đặt mục tiêu quá cao so với khả năng thực hiện.
Một yêu cầu khác là tăng cường cơ chế giám sát. Thay vì chờ hết quý mới đánh giá kết quả, các địa phương cần theo dõi thường xuyên tiến độ thực hiện, kịp thời phát hiện những chỉ tiêu có nguy cơ không đạt để đưa ra giải pháp khắc phục. Tùy điều kiện thực tế, mỗi địa phương có thể thiết lập ban chỉ đạo hoặc cơ chế điều hành phù hợp nhằm nâng cao hiệu quả giám sát.
Theo bà Thảo, các địa phương cũng cần chủ động dự báo những biến động có thể xảy ra, đặc biệt về giá nhiên liệu, nguyên liệu trên thị trường quốc tế. Trên cơ sở đó, xây dựng sẵn các phương án ứng phó để hạn chế tác động đến hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh và bảo đảm tính liên tục của nền kinh tế.
Về dài hạn, tăng trưởng không thể chỉ dựa vào việc gia tăng vốn đầu tư mà cần chú trọng nâng cao giá trị gia tăng. Trong đó, khoa học công nghệ, chuyển đổi số và đổi mới sáng tạo cần được coi trọng hơn trong quá trình xây dựng và triển khai các giải pháp phát triển.
“Tăng trưởng dựa trên khoa học công nghệ là hướng đi giúp tạo ra sự bứt phá nhanh và có tính bền vững”, bà Thảo nhấn mạnh.

articles.title: Inside the Supermassive Debate Over the James Webb Telescope’s ‘Little Red Dots’
articles.text:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
Astronomers built the James Webb Space Telescope to pick up faint light from the first billion years after the Big Bang, a chaotic era when vast swaths of hydrogen and helium gas gathered into the chains of galaxies we see today. Even in the telescope’s first images, astronomers could see a whole zoo of mysterious smears of light.
One batch of objects proved especially difficult to interpret. They glowed blindingly bright, emitting red light with long wavelengths and shining as brilliantly as a whole galaxy. They were tiny, spanning just a pixel. And they were everywhere. A couple appear in almost every image Webb takes. In 2023, researchers started calling them “little red dots.” Astronomers have repeatedly pointed Webb toward the little red dots, wringing precious new information from these pixels of light.
Initially, researchers thought the dots looked kind of like galaxies. Later, they concluded that little red dots look more like the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of most galaxies. These monstrous masses are themselves dark, but their formidable gravity violently vacuums up gas and other nearby matter, generating rings of hot, swirling detritus that completely outshine the stars around them.
Then, in the spring of 2025, two teams of astronomers simultaneously announced observations of a pair of little red dots that were unlike all the rest. In fact, they were unlike any object ever seen.
“In all the millions of [observations] we’ve taken with ground-based telescopes,” said Anna de Graaff, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg, Germany, and head of one group, “there’s nothing that looks like these sources.”
The two teams of astronomers propose that they are looking at a new astronomical object: a topsy-turvy lump of hydrogen that shines with the light of billions of suns while hiding a black hole deep in its core. They call it a “black hole star.”
In a paper posted in September, astronomers took this analysis a step further. They argued that the Webb telescope is witnessing the births of supermassive black holes inside the cores of colossal stars. “There is a fundamentally new phenomenon afoot,” said Rohan Naidu, an astronomer at the University of Hawai’i.
But not everyone agrees with this bold interpretation. It has sparked a flurry of follow-up research and reignited a fierce debate over the nature of these peculiar pinpricks of light. “The field has gotten very polarized,” said Anna-Christina Eilers, an astrophysicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who studies little red dots.
When all you can see is a speck, it’s hard to tell what you’re looking at. All you know about it is its color and brightness. Astronomers first argued that little red dots were distant galaxies on the cosmic horizon, mainly because of their brightness. But galaxies that bright would have to be huge—and there was no known way for them to grow so big in just hundreds of millions of years. Astronomers dubbed them “universe breakers” for the way they seemed to demolish the standard cosmic timeline.
Then they took a closer look. De Graaff led one survey, called Red Unknowns: Bright Infrared Extragalactic Survey (Rubies), and Naidu co-led another survey, called Mirage or Miracle (MOM). These were two of a wave of surveys that trained the Webb telescope on distant objects, including little red dots, for hours at a time. They tabulated precisely what shades of light were coming from each dot and how bright the shades were. This detailed color breakdown, known as a spectrum, told astronomers a far more detailed story than the initial observations had. Different atoms shine in subtly different hues, so the spectrum provided a sense of what the object’s particles were doing.
The bombshell discovery in the little-red-dot spectra was that the colors of hydrogen were smeared out across multiple shades. Usually, seeing such an effect means you’re looking straight at an exposed black hole. Black holes whip hydrogen clouds around them at furious rates, with the clouds emitting slightly different colors depending on their speed. The net effect is that instead of seeing just the hue of hydrogen, you see a range of colors called a broad line. The wider this range, the faster the fastest hydrogen clouds are flying—and the more massive the black hole.
Many astronomers concluded that big black holes dotted the universe, washing out the light of the stars in their host galaxies. As black holes, the little red dots would appear red because dust—grainy stuff much more complicated than gas—was blocking their blue light.
Yet they still seemed weird. Most supermassive black holes flicker as they gulp down chunky streams of gas around them. They also beam powerful x-rays across the universe. Most little red dots seemed to be doing neither of these things.
But that didn’t trouble astronomers much; they expected to see some strangeness during the pandemonium of the early universe. And at least the black holes weren’t breaking any cosmological theories.
Then, in the spring of 2025, de Graaff’s and Naidu’s teams unveiled the two strangest dots yet.
What made these two little red dots exceptional was how red they were. Webb picked up almost no light in the bluer hues of their spectra. And at a particular shade of red, the colors abruptly got much, much brighter. This feature, known as a Balmer break, is something you see when looking at a hot ball of hydrogen gas—typically, certain types of stars or galaxies, which are made of many stars. Deep in a star’s core, nuclear fusion pumps out heat and light, which slowly filters up to the star’s surface. There, hydrogen atoms can become energized in a way that blocks bluer light and lets through only redder light. These red colors have a hump-shaped spectrum that reveals the overall temperature of the star’s surface.
But the new little red dots couldn’t literally be stars—they were way too bright. And they didn’t look much like black holes either. Black holes have an assortment of ringlike structures of different temperatures. They don’t typically produce a Balmer break, or the red, hump-shaped curve indicative of a stellar surface burning at a uniform 5,000 or so degrees Kelvin.
Naidu and de Graaff concluded that they were looking at the first examples of something combining the vigor of a black hole with the outward appearance of a star: a black hole star.
From the outside, a black hole star would appear as a huge agglomeration of hydrogen gas. If our sun were replaced with a black hole star, it would extend a dozen times farther than the orbit of Pluto. Out toward the edge, the star would boil unstably, sloughing off outer layers and explosively ejecting mass. “It’s going to be a very messy system where stuff is being blown out and falling back in,” de Graaff said. “I wouldn’t want to come too close.”
Deep in the center, invisible to the outside world, the star would be powered by a black hole. This black hole would pull gas around it, dramatically heating it and pushing light and energy outward, which would keep the outer layers of hydrogen from collapsing inward. In this way, the black hole would form the “engine” of the star, analogous to the fusion-powered core of our sun. Moving outward, material swirling around the black hole would beam out a range of colors that would slowly make their way toward the surface.
And as with certain stars, the hydrogen near the surface would stop the bluer light while letting the redder light pass through. The end result would be a gassy surface shining as brightly as a more exposed black hole but with the Balmer break and smooth red hump of a 5,000-kelvin star, de Graaff and Naidu theorized. As a bonus, the gas “cocoon” would also block x-rays, and the gas wouldn’t flicker much—which would explain two mysteries surrounding other little red dots.
But what about the broad lines, supposedly caused by hydrogen swirling fast around a black hole? Another group provided a possible explanation.
That group, which included Vadim Rusakov, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, had been scrutinizing the broad lines of the best-observed little red dots. Broad lines take the shape of a sharp mountain peak. But Rusakov and collaborators noticed that in many cases, these mountains sloped slightly more gently than would be expected if they came from fast-moving gas around a black hole. So they suggested that instead of coming from rotating gas, much of the spread of the hydrogen colors could come from light scattering off electrons.
They digitally removed the effect of this electron-induced smudging from their data, Rusakov said. After that, the broad lines stopped looking quite so broad and started looking more like light passing through a sluggishly churning shell of hydrogen gas in a particular state, similar to what you’d expect to see from a black hole star. The three teams—de Graaff’s, Naidu’s, and Rusakov’s — posted their findings on March 20, 2025—“black hole star date,” as some of the researchers called it.
Black hole stars could represent a new stage in the development of a supermassive black hole: First, a black hole would form in the center of a shell of hydrogen, together with a baby galaxy of normal stars around it. Then, over time, the black hole would eat its way out of its cocoon, gaining mass as it cleared the hydrogen gas away.
“We are seeing the seed,” Naidu said. “This is the birth of potentially every massive black hole in the universe.”
The black hole star enthusiasts appeal to Occam’s razor, arguing that their theory gives the simplest accounting of these two little red dots, and perhaps of little red dots in general. But simple is subjective, and astronomers have spent the last year in a lively debate about what’s really going on.
Even years after the discovery of the first little red dot, not much about them is settled. Dale Kocevski, an astrophysicist at Colby College, recalls leading a discussion about them at an April 2026 conference in Aspen, Colorado. He started by recapping what he hoped would be an uncontroversial idea about their trace amounts of blue light. “The group erupted into argument, and we couldn’t even get past the first bullet point,” he said.
Many astronomers still argue that little red dots are traditional black holes—even the new duo. “The data is really compelling,” said Roberto Maiolino of the University of Cambridge. “I’m a little bit more dubious about the interpretation.”
For each point in favor of black hole stars, Maiolino fires off a quick rebuttal. The lack of flicker? In the early universe, black holes may have had a steadier food supply and may therefore have been tidier eaters. The lack of x-rays? Standard galactic black holes are ringed by a thick doughnut of gas and dust, which can block most x-rays. He sees no reason to suspect the little red dots of being anything other than standard supermassive black holes.
The redness of the new objects is striking, he said, and he agrees that it means there must be a ton of gas between the black hole and us. But that gas could come in the form of the doughnut, or as puffy clouds that fill in patches of the black hole’s sky, as opposed to the shell of gas around a black hole star. Maiolino agrees that electron scattering likely contributes to broadening the lines in the spectra of some of the little red dots. But electron scattering also smears hydrogen lines from supermassive black holes, he said.
Maiolino and his collaborator, Piero Madau of the University of California, Santa Cruz, argue that the redness of the dots comes mainly from the angle at which we see them. The reddest dots are those that we happen to see edge on, their gassy doughnuts blocking our view. Webb also sees some “little blue dots.” These could be the same exposed black holes, viewed top-down, Maiolino and Madau pointed out in spring 2026. They also appeal to Occam’s razor—in this case arguing that black holes are a simpler explanation for little dots of all colors.
At this stage either theory—black hole or black hole star—could match what the Webb telescope has seen. “I don’t think that there is a compelling reason to prefer one or the other,” said Mauro Giavalisco, an astronomer at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, who has spent much of his career interpreting the spectra of distant galaxies.
To test their interpretations, astronomers need a clearer picture of how black hole stars might form and how exactly they expect them to look.
Over the last few years, Mitchell Begelman has been teaching a graduate student seminar on little red dots at the University of Colorado, Boulder. It’s kept him reading the firehose of papers coming out on the subject. In these mysterious objects that weren’t quite stars and weren’t quite black holes, he recognized a ghost from his past: the quasi-star. “Suddenly the switch flipped, and I realized that this is what quasi-stars should look like,” Begelman said.
Begelman had proposed the existence of quasi-stars back in 2006, along with Marta Volonteri and Martin Rees, to explain observations of what looked like impossibly massive black holes. Their quasi-star theory offers one way to make a black hole star: The core of a vast gas cloud collapses to directly form a black hole, gathering the remainder of the cloud around it.
In 2025, Begelman and his collaborator Jason Dexter applied the quasi-star model to the little red dots. They estimated that quasi-stars could quickly assemble themselves in a few million years before settling into a more mature form that would look just like little red dots. They would do this for tens of millions of years—lasting long enough for Webb to spot them.
In 2026, Giavalisco worked with a team to flesh out the quasi-star model as an origin for black hole stars, which he finds to be a natural way of explaining how little red dots could mask the signs of a feeding black hole. He points out that our sun performs the same trick, hiding its explosive fusion, just on a much smaller scale. “We have billions and billions of hydrogen bombs exploding every second, and yet we see none of them,” he said.
Giavalisco and his collaborators found that their new model of a quasi-star fit the spectra of de Graaf’s and Naidu’s objects even better than the initial models had. He thinks the quasi-star theory is a plausible explanation for the little red dots but remains open to other ideas. “I just want to know the truth,” he said.
In the meantime, researchers are starting to search for another distinguishing pattern: If little red dots are black hole stars formed in the early universe, then they should grow rarer over time as they each break free from their shells and reveal their inner black holes.
In an August 2026 census of both red and blue dots broken up into different eras, Kocevski of Colby College and his collaborators found exactly that pattern. In the data, as the universe approaches 2 billion to 3 billion years of age, the little red dots seem to vanish—preliminary evidence that little red dots, as black hole stars, might really be a puberty-like phase for many supermassive black holes.
Theorists are already working out what that puberty-like phase might be like. In another analysis, posted on September 8, Naidu, de Graaff, Eilers, and their collaborators tested out an assortment of techniques for deducing the mass of a black hole “seed” inside a black hole star. These hidden black holes seemed to be far less massive than standard, exposed black holes. The scientists propose that Webb is catching supermassive black hole stars—up to 1 million times the mass of the sun—in the act of incubating the universe’s first big black holes.
Some researchers, including Kocevski, still aren’t sure. Kocevski suspects that the universe is a messy place, and that some little red dots are truly as starlike as the black hole star camp is arguing. Others, he thinks, will be more like standard black holes, as the other camp argues. “I have a sneaking suspicion that we’re both right,” he said.

articles.title: It’s time to find a new browser
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 149, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy It Actually Feels Like Fall Now At Least In My Neighborhood), and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
It’s time to find a new browser
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Call of Duty is back, Kindle Plus is sort of new, and you need to watch Wildwood.
This week, I’ve been reading about Demis Hassabis and computer chips and permafrost, enjoying the first episodes of Machine Gods,filming the next season of Version History (pet season!), seeing You Can See Everythingand then reading and listening to absolutely everything about it, painstakingly updating all the stuff in my 1Password, making tiny documents with Tiny Little Office, watching Conan O’Brien own Subway Takesthe way he once owned Hot Ones,finally getting properly good at CapCut, and blasting the soundtrack to The Mandalorian and Grogu all workday long.
I also have for you a new AI assistant, the most Duo-y new app for the iPhone Duo, my hunt for the next great browser, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you playing / reading / watching / listening to / modding with Claude this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Obviously, Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest game release of the year, but a new COD is always a big deal. This one doesn’t sound like some grand reinvention of the form, but rather an even more playable, even more powerful version of what works. I was particularly excited to hear that the campaign mode is a huge improvement this time.
- The Blink Mini 4K. Ring cameras get a lot more shine, but Amazon’s cheaper brand also makes some pretty good stuff. This one’s part of a whole new lineup of devices, but $80 for a 4K camera with two-way audio and plenty of smart security features? Not a bad deal.
- JustWatch TV. As streaming services get incessantly more expensive, I’m starting to bail on some paid services and spend more time on the free ones. JustWatch’s new service is surprisingly well-stocked out of the gate — I suspect they’ve been watching what people search for, and making some smart content bets.
- Claude Duet. Here’s Anthropic’s answer to Muse, Instinct, and Dots. Duet seems to be focused on helping you get stuff done at work by making to-do lists, coordinating meetings, and compiling data for you. Still waitlist-only right now, but it’ll be interesting to see if it’s as thirsty for attention as Muse is.
- Wildwood. Before you see this gorgeous, by all accounts excellent stop-motion movie, read everything you can about how it was made. Not a pixel of generative AI in sight, just an unbelievable amount of hard work and human creativity. Humans rock, artists rock, this movie rocks.
- The Teenage Engineering EP-35. When you go to buy this thing, it’s technically called “Life is fantastic!” Which, sure. This thing is a battery powered, multi-input, multi-instrument amp with lots of effects. As always, it is extremely cool-looking. I have no use for it, and I want it quite badly.
- Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. Nintendo basically hasn’t changed the formula here since Wii Sports from two decades ago, and I have absolutely no problem with that. Anything that gives me that super-active tennis and bowling (plus volleyball, boxing, thumb wrestling, and more) is a win in my book.
- Delta 2.0. The next couple of weeks are going to be full of interesting app updates as developers try to figure out what to make of Apple’s foldable phone. But one of the best is already available; Delta can now pretty successfully cosplay as any handheld console ever. (Plus the Sega Genesis!)
- Kindle Plus. This is mostly just a rebranding of Kindle Unlimited, but Amazon put a couple of interesting new features in its $12 monthly reading subscription, including AI-narrated audiobooks. I am dubious of those, but excited about expanding access to audiobooks. We’ll see.
Spotlight
The worst news of the week here in the Installerverse is that Arc is going away. This was obviously coming: The Browser Company bailed on Arc two years ago in favor of the more AI-centric Dia, and Arc has been in maintenance mode ever since. But now it’s not just being ignored, it’s going away. By Christmas, you won’t even be able to use the app anymore.
So now a lot of us are stuck looking for another browser. There are a million new ones out there, many of them somewhere between “heavily inspired by Arc” and “a direct copy of Arc I made in Codex this morning.” I need to test a lot of them. I don’t know exactly where I’ll land yet, but I figured I’d share a bunch of the ones I’m looking at:
- Dia. It has recently gotten a lot of Arc’s best features, and some of the AI stuff is pretty cool. (And mercifully easy to turn off.) The Browser Company’s attention to aesthetic detail remains the best in the biz, so I’m starting here.
- Zen. A total ripoff of Arc, and I mean that as a compliment. Zen runs on Mozilla’s Gecko engine rather than Chromium, which is a win for anyone looking for a little less Google influence in their lives. Last time I tried Zen it was a little buggy and unpolished, but I’ve heard it’s come a long way.
- Orion. I am a dedicated and very happy Kagi user, and I’ve heard good things about how simple and resource-friendly the company’s browser is. Given the seamless Kagi integration, I sort of hope this one wins for me.
- Vivaldi. I used Vivaldi for a while, and I love how customizable it is. I eventually got it set up exactly the way I wanted it. But right next to all that customization is just a feeling of fiddliness, and I couldn’t quite get comfortable in the browser. Might try again.
- Helium. The opposite of Vivaldi, this is a super minimalist, no-frills browser. It’s probably what I need, honestly.
- Firefox. Its confusing stance on AI aside, I like a lot of the recent design and feature choices Firefox has made. I’m also intrigued by some of the Firefox forks, like Waterfox and Floorp, which give it even more customization options.
- Brave. Brave has always felt too heavy to me, and like it’s always trying to convince me to use more of its own proprietary (and often underpowered) features. But it seems to always win in privacy comparisons, so I might need to give it a go again.
On mobile, it’s easy. Quiche is my favorite iOS browser by a mile. Arc was never great on Android, so I’m betting most of us never switched there in the first place.
There are also the default browsers, of course, like Chrome, Safari, and Edge. But each of those browsers continues to fail me in one way or another, and so my search continues. If you’ve found your browser of the future, tell me all about it! Otherwise, I’ll report back here periodically through my journey.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Youth is an absolute SCREAM on HBO Max at the moment.” — Jonathan
“Todoist has a stellar integration with Siri AI that has finally made me fully commit to just using it If you delete Reminders, Todoist becomes the default on Siri AI and you can add a to-do to any project with tag AND location support (using Apple Maps saved locations like home and work!). The best part is that it all works WITHOUT having to say ‘... in todoist’ at the end of each query!” — Sajishnu
“Apple added Sound Glow to existing HomePod models and it’s just kinda fun to watch the light on top of HomePod glow and flash. So I’m doing that with some of my favorite playlists.” — Connor
“I’m reading a book called How to Read a Book by Mortimer J. Adler because I want to get better at analysis and reading for understanding vs. absorbing basic information.” — Rhoades
“My girlfriend took a train ride up the west coast and reported that no less than four different people asked her if her 2024 Samsung Galaxy Z-Flip 6 was the new iPhone Duo.” — Nicholas
“I recently read Bodies of Magic by Freya Marske, and it was excellent. What if med school was magical, but everyone was still sleeping with each other and stressing over student loans? Then an unexpected dead body shows up during finals.” — Emmett
“I got a Framework Laptop 13 Pro running Ubuntu last month, and I’m really happy with it. (I haven’t done anything with Linux in maybe 20 years — it’s come a long way!) So now I’m trying to see if I can replace Capture One with Darktable. If I can, that would break my last tie to macOS, and I’ll replace my iMac with a Framework Desktop.” — Morgan
“Exploring the new Nektropos Castle dungeon in EverQuest Legends. The game has been such a nostalgia trip back to 1999, but new content in an ancient game is a bizarre delight.” — Alex
“Setting up Navidrome and having Claude build me a definitive ‘Songs From the Black Hole’ playlist from my Weezer MP3 collection. (It’s harder than first appears: is ‘Lisa’ track 12 or not!?)” — Micheal
“Best Buy had a pretty insane deal on a Bambu A1 Mini, so we got my 12 year old son a 3D printer for his birthday. It’s amazing how easy it was to put out a seemingly perfectly accurate PLA print, compared to horror stories from older printers.” — Jeff
Signing off
Last week, my wife and I went car shopping. Our plan was just to drive a bunch of cars — we knew we needed something with three rows, and really had no experience with any of them — and then go home. Somehow, a few hours later, we were the proud and slightly bewildered owners of a new Kia Carnival.
So far the car has been great, but wow are there a lot of weird tech ideas in cars now. I’m good with CarPlay and Android Auto. I hate how much everything has become a touchscreen. But I’m most thrown by how many features of my car now exist in a companion app. How do we feel about this? I almost miss when I had no idea what to do about the check engine light.
Anyway, I’m a minivan dad now. I think I’m okay with it. Send car tips! Send minivan tips! Send help! See you next week!

articles.title: Meta is delaying its controversial new business terms amid scraping concerns - Engadget
articles.text:
Meta is delaying its controversial new business terms amid scraping concerns
The new terms were supposed to take effect on October 30.
Meta's controversial new commercial terms of use won't be taking effect on October 30 after all. In an email sent to Reuters and Fast Company, a spokesperson said that the company was "extending the effective date of [its] updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to 20 November to allow more time... to explain to [its] partners and stakeholders what's changing and what's not."
If you'll recall, the company previously shared a planned update to its terms with language saying that Meta would have the right to use web scrapers and automated tools "to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them)" associated with business accounts on the platform. The updated terms would also state that Meta "may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features.
After publishers and other businesses raised concerns, the company changed its language to remove the reference to AI training. Since then, potentially affected entities have submitted complaints to antitrust authorities about the updated terms. The News Media Alliance, which represents thousands of news media organizations in the United States and in Canada, also sent the company an open letter, demanding that it withdraw its revised terms of use before October 30. "News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation," the organization wrote.
Meta added in its statement that it will explain to its partners how it uses its web crawlers and make it clear that content owners and publishers will be able to use robots.txt. The plain text file will be able to signal the content owners' preferences to crawlers and AI bots and stop them from indexing their content. That said, Reuters previously reported that multiple AI companies' crawlers regularly ignore robots.txt instructions.

articles.title: Democrats, voting-rights groups challenge Trump's bid to block Alaska Senate certification
articles.text:
Democratic groups and voting-rights advocates are seeking to join a federal lawsuit to stop the Justice Department's effort to prevent Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The requests come from Alaskans for Mary, the campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, the Democratic Party's Senate campaign committee, and a separate group including the League of Women Voters of Alaska, Common Cause and two individual voters.
Together, the groups argue that the executive branch lacks legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration with early voting already underway.
In court filings submitted Friday, the groups contend that the litigation — which President Donald Trump confirmed he personally ordered — seeks an extraordinary remedy: an investigation into whether voters who selected another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan actually intended to vote for the incumbent senator.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he directed the Justice Department to file the lawsuit: "I'm the one that said 'do it.'"
The move drew swift bipartisan backlash, including from Alaska's Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who said on social media, "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."
Two Sullivans
The legal battle centers on Daniel J. Sullivan, a non-incumbent challenger sharing a near-identical name with incumbent GOP Senator Daniel S. Sullivan. Alaska election officials initially removed the challenger from the ballot after a complaint from the state Republican Party, but state courts ordered his inclusion on the ballot.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that decision and directed election officials to clearly distinguish the two men.
The ballot now lists Sen. Sullivan as the "incumbent" and Republican, while the other Sullivan has no party registration.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct. 22, seeking an order to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election if the incumbent loses.
The proposed intervenors say the department's approach would force Alaska voters to choose between electing the president's preferred candidate and risking the state being barred from certifying its election results.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argue that the lawsuit directly threatens their interests because it could prevent Peltola from taking office even if she wins the election under Alaska's ranked-choice system.
They also question whether Alaska state officials will mount a sufficiently vigorous defense, given that the state's Division of Elections previously tried to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot before a state court overturned the move.
The DSCC and Alaskans for Mary are asking the court to grant them defendant-intervenor status so they can formally file motions to dismiss the lawsuit.
Severe hazards
The Democrats argue that while the DOJ has cited the National Voter Registration Act as the legal basis for its lawsuit, the statute contains no provision authorizing the federal government to dictate candidate eligibility or ballot layout, which are state matters under the Constitution.
Legal experts have echoed those concerns, noting that relying on the NVRA's general preamble language to halt state election certification lacks precedent.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause filed separately, warning that the DOJ's demand to investigate voter intent presents severe constitutional hazards.
The filings note that the DOJ has offered no mechanism to determine whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan intended to vote for the incumbent.
Blocking certification, the groups argue, would disenfranchise Alaskans by denying them representation and injecting chaos into the election outcome.
Both organizations are asking the court for permission to join the case as defendants. The Democratic groups say they intend to seek dismissal if the court grants their motion.

articles.title: AI funding fears rattle Wall Street. Here's how we're adjusting our portfolio
articles.text: Wall Street struggled to find its footing last week as renewed concerns about financing the artificial intelligence boom overshadowed strong earnings. An early rebound in AI-related names ran into a brick wall Thursday after Meta Platforms reported negative free cash flow for the first time since its 2012 initial public offering. The sell-off spread to more defensive areas of the market Friday, sending the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% as oil prices surged on fears of renewed U.S. strikes against Iran. The Nasdaq only posted a slight loss as investors returned to beaten-down chip stocks and bought up cyber stocks. The S & P 500 on Friday was modestly lower. For the week, the Dow was the big winner, rising 0.4%. The S & P 500 was down 0.5%, while the Nasdaq slipped 0.7%. Here's a closer look at the three developments that drove last week's market action. AI funding fears deepen The AI trade remained volatile last week as investors weighed strong demand against growing concerns about how companies will finance the massive infrastructure buildout. AI stocks rallied early in the week, especially on SpaceX 's surging revenue numbers reported Tuesday evening . Thursday was terrible. In addition to cash flow concerns, Meta's strong earnings from Wednesday evening were overshadowed by its disclosure that its long-term plans could require hundreds of billions of dollars in additional financing. CoreWeave , which has become a focal point for concerns about debt-fueled AI spending, fell 10% Thursday as investors continued to scrutinize its borrowing costs. It was down more than 10% for the week after the neocloud ended the prior week down more than 25%. Even Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged the funding challenge, saying Thursday that the "demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital." The issue isn't AI demand, but whether companies can secure enough financing to meet it as borrowing becomes more expensive. Nvidia was down roughly 1.5% last week. We took advantage of Thursday's sell-off to buy 10 shares of GE Vernova , our first AI-related purchase in five weeks, and upgraded the stock to our buy-equivalent 1 rating on confidence in long-term power demand. But we also reduced our exposure to the broader AI trade. "The collapse of the data center requires us to circle the wagons," Jim Cramer said. "We can't have too much of the ones we have. We can pick as we did with GEV, but nothing aggressive. And all tag ends should go like Broadcom." He continued: "Circling means we want to be bigger in the better ones." To that end, we exited Broadcom on Friday, locking in an average gain of roughly 128%. We also trimmed CrowdStrike , realizing a gain of about 187%, to right-size the position rather than because of concerns about its fundamentals. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks were our two biggest winners last week — both up more than 11% as news of the security flaws in the PHP programming language touched off a global security scramble. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz told CNBC Friday that AI-powered attacks observed by CrowdStrike doubled each month from July through September. Jim has said all along that cyber is needed more than ever in the new world of AI. Unpacking Meta's wild week Meta delivered a strong third quarter Wednesday evening, but worries about negative free cash flow and its AI spending needs upstaged strong guidance and a promising roadmap for its viral Muse AI agent. What made Thursday's 7% drop in Meta shares even more painful was that it had been rallying in after-hours trading on Wednesday night on encouraging signs for Muse. While a muted capital expenditure outlook was initially viewed as a positive on earnings night, a regulatory filing from Meta quickly raised fresh concerns about its funding needs. The company warned that its long-term plans could require raising "hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026." The filing shed more light on Meta's plan to create a new class of non-voting stock, Class C, in January to help finance investments and acquisitions without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting control. The new share class would basically facilitate a two-for-one stock split, with holders getting one Class C share for every Class A they own. While encouraged by early Muse traction and Meta's strong core digital advertising business, we want greater clarity on how those investments will be funded and monetized. We maintained our hold-equivalent 2 rating on Meta stock and $800 price target. Meta stock lost more than 9% on the week. Bright spots in the portfolio The rotation out of AI stocks benefited several defensive portfolio holdings last week, reinforcing the importance of diversification . Kimberly-Clark jumped 4.3% as investors sought safety in consumer staples. Home Depot increased 3.3%, benefiting from the 10-year Treasury yield going below 5%, which could help revive housing activity and home improvement spending. Johnson & Johnson surged 3.2%, recovering all its post-earnings losses as investors rotated into healthcare. There were also encouraging developments for Apple and Qnity Electronics . Apple's new foldable iPhone Duo is off to a strong start, with delivery wait times exceeding three months. While supply constraints are contributing to the delays, strong demand suggests the device could become another growth engine. The Duo became available in stores for walk-in customers on Friday. Apple shares rose about 1.2% for the week. The iPhone maker also expanded its partnership with Qnity , which will produce advanced films for the 18 Pro's new camera system. The deeper relationship is encouraging, though our investment thesis remains centered on Qnity's fast-growing data center business. Qnity shares fell more than 4.5% for the week on the recent data center trade troubles, though far less than GE Vernova's over 11% weekly drop. Watch out video tour of Qnity labs outside Boston. (See here for a full list of the stocks in Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade.
