articles.title: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections
articles.text:
U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.
A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report, and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well.
The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.
Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June.
Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report.
The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.
Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.

articles.title: Retail investors are not more sophisticated than 30 years ago, says former hedge fund manager
articles.text:
Retail investors who are trying to beat the market by buying individual stocks and complex exchange-traded funds may be better off with broad market index funds, according to Elm Wealth's Victor Haghani.
"I'm not sure that investors are that much more sophisticated than they were 30 years ago," the firm's founder and chief investment officer told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "We still are human beings and we're subject to certain kinds of biases — particularly extrapolation bias where whatever has happened recently in the past we tend to believe that it's going to continue into the future."
Haghani, who was a founding partner at hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, emphasizes cost-effective investment strategies as a priority at his current firm.
"It's an environment that continues to be tough for individual non-professionals to generate alpha," he said. "[Retail investors are] just very well served by having some exposure to broader index funds overall."
According to Haghani, access to elaborate strategies doesn't necessarily provide advantages.
"Whether it's Citadel or Jane Street or Hudson River Trading, they're just minting money every single day. So, it's an opportunity-rich environment — if you happen to have a billion dollars to spend on tech each year," he said. "If you're a retail investor sitting at home and trying to find opportunities, you have to realize that probably on the other side of your trades is [Citadel CEO] Ken Griffin or whoever, and it's probably not going to end all that well."
'More choice is ultimately a good thing'
However, RBC Capital Markets' Valerie Grimba sees sophisticated funds playing a strategic role in retail investors' portfolios.
"More choice is ultimately a good thing," the firm's director of global ETF strategy said in the same interview.
She said funds holding 10 to 15 stocks can help investors participate in specific investment themes without having to identify their eventual biggest winner, while derivative-based products can be used to generate income in various ways.
But Grimba also emphasized that investors need to understand the holdings and trade-offs of the strategies they choose.
"It's more important than ever for an individual investor to understand what they're buying," she said. "You should be able to explain to your friend what it is in the ETF and what you're buying."

articles.title: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'
articles.text:
One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.
It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA and navigating the next chapter of my career with a focus on prestige and financial success.
But soon after relocating from Kentucky to California in October 2021, I burned out. I had transitioned into a remote healthcare marketing role, living on the West Coast but still working East Coast hours and completing my second year of business school from afar. While everyone around me seemed to be heading to the beach and enjoying the sunshine, I spent my days inside, glued to a computer screen.
The dog walker I followed online seemed to have everything I was craving: fresh air, movement, flexibility and a job that didn't revolve around emails and Zoom meetings.
During a long drive, I joked with my husband, "I think I'm going to quit my job and walk dogs." The joke quickly became a plan.
My season as a professional dog walker
Within the span of just a few weeks in the spring of 2022, I quit my job, graduated from business school, traveled to Europe for an old roommate's wedding and then flew to Texas to speak at the Latino Franchise Symposium. While I was there, I created my Rover profile. I highlighted my experience volunteering at animal shelters in college, pet sitting for friends and caring for animals throughout my life.
Before I even made it back home to California, I had my first meet-and-greet scheduled with a potential client. Shortly after, I landed my first booking. I was thrilled.
At first, I intentionally priced my services below what seemed typical in my area to build reviews, charging about $15 for a drop-in visit and about $17 for a 30-minute walk. Some days I had just one client. I was able to start small because I had savings to tide me over, along with a partner whose job provided steady income and benefits.
Still, I treated it like a real business from day one. I accepted nearly every opportunity that came my way, taking dogs on midday walks, housesitting on weekends and boarding dogs in my apartment.
I sent thoughtful updates to the dog owners filled with photos, detailed notes and plenty of emojis. I shared bathroom break tallies, funny moments and anything unusual they should know. If I stayed overnight, I brought in packages, cleaned up after myself and made sure their home looked exactly as they had left it.
My goal wasn't simply to complete the booking. It was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.
The reviews started rolling in. As my profile gained traction, I gradually increased my rates, eventually charging $23 for a drop-in visit and $84 for overnight stays. By the time I left the platform four months later, I had earned a five-star rating with 30 reviews, built a roster of recurring clients and filled my calendar.
One of my favorite memories came when a family asked me to care for their dogs during their wedding weekend. I spent two and a half days at a beautiful resort and dressed the dogs in tiny tuxedos before they walked down the aisle.
It reminded me that this work was about helping families enjoy some of the biggest moments of their lives with peace of mind. Years later, we're still friends. They now have a daughter, and my daughter and I recently attended her first birthday party.
A new definition of success
Some days I walked more than eight miles, logging over 18,000 steps as I explored neighborhoods I otherwise never would have discovered. I spent hours outside instead of sitting behind a desk. Sometimes I listened to podcasts or music. Other times, I simply enjoyed the quiet.
Those walks gave me space to think. I reflected on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.
Before Rover, success meant getting promotions, landing bigger clients and climbing the corporate ladder. Walking dogs challenged that definition. I realized I didn't want to chase an impressive title as much as I wanted to chase a lifestyle that gave me energy.
Ironically, it was during one of those walks that I received the phone call offering me the marketing job I still have today. I paused on the sidewalk, accepted the offer and then finished the walk.
Returning to marketing wasn't a difficult decision. By then, I was pregnant with my first daughter and needed the stability, benefits and predictable income that came with a full-time role. When an excited dog chasing a squirrel pulled me to the ground early in my pregnancy, it became clear that my season as a professional dog walker was coming to an end.
Still, I think about those four months often. People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had.
It reminded me that passion is visible, no matter what kind of work you're doing. It reinforced that the skills that matter most — showing up, listening, caring deeply, building trust and making small, consistent changes — translate to every career.
And even though I'm back in marketing, my days look different than they did before my dog-walking era. These days, you'll find me logging off at 5 p.m. to go play outside with my family before dinner, walking near the ocean after a hard week, having kitchen dance parties to shake off the day, taking calls while walking my own dog or squeezing in a lunchtime workout. The fresh air and sense of presence give me the balance I craved when I was glued to screens on a schedule dictated by someone else's time zone.
Those four months taught me something my MBA never could: Success isn't just about finding a job that sounds impressive. It's about building a life you genuinely enjoy living, even if it doesn't look like the one you originally imagined.
Sally Simmons is a marketing leader and holistic health coach based in California. After years building strategies for global brands, she found unexpected lessons about business, connection and success during a four-month chapter as a professional dog walker. Today, she brings those lessons into her work helping people create healthier, more balanced lives.

articles.title: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
articles.text:
A drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca, a study found.
Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.
The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.
That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed.
"I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.
The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility."
The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.
Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.
Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.
He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years.
Using Imdelltra earlier
Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.
Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone.
Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.
Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it.
Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer.
Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.
The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches.
Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own.
She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread.
In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since.
"I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

articles.title: An ex-bookkeeper spent $375 to launch a sewing business: 'I hadn't felt so sure about something like that in a long time'
articles.text:
Eric Lugo didn't know that when he launched his sewing workshop business, Stitch Lab ATX, as a side project in May 2025, it'd become his full-time focus within weeks.
Lugo also couldn't have predicted it'd become so successful within two years that offerings would grow fivefold, classes would regularly sell out and he'd start getting requests to host private events.
The idea came to him a few years ago: Lugo learned to sew from his grandma when he was 5 and got serious about it as a teen, eventually launching his fashion brand, Casa Amiré, and becoming his friends' go-to guy for tailoring and alterations help. Dresses needed hemming, jeans needed shortening. Lugo was happy to lend his talents, though the requests piled up.
So one day, in April 2024, he thought: What if he taught his friends how to fix their clothes themselves?
"It really made me think: Wow, this is — I think — a pretty important skill that a lot of people don't know how to do," Lugo, 29, of Austin, Texas, tells CNBC Make It. He could fill that gap. "I think I have enough knowledge after you know 14 [or] 15 years to be able to teach other people, and so I went from there."
A $375 investment
For months, while in between jobs and selling wares from his fashion brand, Lugo couldn't stop thinking about launching a sewing workshop. Around August 2024, he got a bookkeeping job for a local PR firm and shelved the idea. But by the beginning of 2025, it was back on his mind. He mapped out the classes he'd offer and how he'd get the word out.
By April, Lugo put money into it. He spent $375 to buy eight sewing machines, sourced second-hand from Facebook Marketplace, and set up shop in a friend's warehouse space that wasn't in use outside of business hours. Lugo gathered friends and family members to test-run his curriculum.
Stitch Lab ATX held its first classes in early May, Lugo says, with a few sign-ups for one-on-one private lessons and a handful of students taking his "crash course" workshop covering beginner-friendly basics, like learning how to thread a machine and sewing a straight line.
Then Lugo's circumstances changed fast: Toward the end of May, he was let go from his day job. It wasn't a question that he'd go all-in on his studio.
"Not even 10 minutes after I had just gotten laid off and gotten off of that Zoom meeting, I called my boy that has the warehouse, and I said, 'Dude, I just got laid off. Are you cool with me just going full-send with Stitch Lab?'" Lugo says. His friend was 100% in.
"I honestly hadn't felt so sure about something like that in a long time, if ever," Lugo says.
A rise in DIY hobbies
It took some time for things to get moving.
By his count, Lugo held around four to six classes in those early months. Sometimes just two or three people would show up, even though he could host up to 10. Lugo says demand picked up around September 2025 once he started partnering with local businesses to host pop-up sewing events (like a sip-and-stitch at a brewery) and spreading the word on TikTok.
Today the lab offers around two dozen classes per month and can fill up quickly when spots open up a month in advance, Lugo says.
Sessions typically cost $65 to $85 and last about two-and-a-half hours. Classes range from beginner-friendly lessons, like learning how to use a machine, to teaching intermediate skills, like hemming pants or installing a zipper. Students can sign up for special workshops to make a specific project, like a flower tote, or book open sewing time at the warehouse space. Lugo also takes requests to teach at special events, like for a bachelorette party or corporate offsite, averaging about one a month.
Lugo says he draws a salary from the business, which is his primary source of income.
Stitch Lab's success coincides with a trend of many Americans paying up to invest in their hobbies, even as the costs of goods and materials rise, leading to a trend of what Bank of America refers to as "funflation." Spending on hobbies, ranging from arts and crafts and hobby shops to retailers selling skiing, hiking, camping or scuba diving gear, grew 7.9% in August 2026 from the year prior, according to the bank's analysis of its card data.
To help some students offset these costs, Lugo in August began a monthly giveaway initiative called Sew It Forward, where entrants can comment on a Stitch Lab social media post about why they want to learn to sew, for the chance to win a free new sewing machine, supplies and a free class with the studio.
"I'm thankful for the support that I've received," Lugo says, "and so I want to put all that back into the community now that I'm in a position to do so."
A growing sewing community
Stitch Lab also stands out during a time when people, especially young adults, are craving community-oriented, offline social events. There's even a resurgence of so-called "grandma hobbies," like knitting and scrapbooking, as people seek relaxing pastimes that keep them off their phones.
In the warehouse dotted with sewing machines and early 2000s or reggaeton music streaming from the sound system, Lugo says he aims to build Stitch Lab up as a fun, creative "judgment-free zone" that can "feel like a home for people."
As an Afro-Latino founder, he says, "this is a safe space for Latinos, for people of color."
"I think community is needed, especially today with so much that's happening in the world," he adds. "No matter who you are, where you come from, you have a safe space to be around other people, learn the same thing ... and just have fun."
Stitch Lab ATX's future plans are already taking shape. Lugo says he just hired two part-time instructors to his team, which will allow them to expand to upward of 30 workshops per month. He still aims to keep classes relatively intimate to support one-on-one help and small-group socializing.
Lugo even sees his business expanding beyond Austin, with his sights set on New York City, hotspots across California and even Mexico City.
"I just want to continue to do what I'm doing all around the world," he says.

articles.title: Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom
articles.text:
Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).
Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.
"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.
Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.
Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.
"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."
Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.
The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.
The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.
Innovating is paying off
Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.
Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).
While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.
Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.
Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.
Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.
High-tech tools and M&A
Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.
Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.
Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.
On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.
Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.
One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.
It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.
GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.
Where to invest in biotech now
ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.
The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.
Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."
Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.
Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.
Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.
In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.
The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.
Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.
Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.
The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."
Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.
Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.
Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.
T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

articles.title: Fact vs. fiction: Doctors share whether peptides are safe and effective
articles.text:
From YouTube influencers to Reddit threads, the health and wellness side of the internet is full of talk about peptides.
The term refers to a class of chemical compounds made up of short chains of amino acids. In the wellness market, synthetic peptides are often sold to consumers as injectables, which some health influencers say can bring a wide range of health benefits from muscle recovery and longevity to improved sexual function. Some peptides, including GLP-1 drugs commonly used for weight loss or diabetes, are heavily researched and federally approved for medical use. Many other forms of peptides are not.
Yet even some lightly researched peptides may be on their way to pharmacy shelves. The Department of Health and Human Services is reportedly planning to allow specialty pharmacies to compound certain synthetic peptides that have the support of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who told podcaster Joe Rogan that he is a "big fan" of the injectables in a February 2026 interview. As reported, the move would be an interim access policy covering some specific peptides not currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
Such a move would be controversial from a regulatory point of view: Multiple peptides, including one of the compounds reportedly included in the health department's proposal, appear on an FDA list of injectables that "may present significant safety risks." That compound, known as BPC-157, has shown potential anti-inflammatory effects in some animal and lab studies but has not yet been subject to large-scale human testing for safety or effectiveness.
"There are a few reasons why, but one of the main ones is the absence of evidence," including robust human studies on safety and effectiveness, says Dr. Caleb Alexander, a professor of epidemiology and medicine at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Yet consumer interest and regulatory momentum for peptides are growing. So here's what you need to know about peptides, from why they're the subject of such conversation to whether or not they're safe or effective to use.
What are peptides?
Peptides are "kind of like the building blocks of proteins," says Dr. Alison Dempsey, a dermatologist at the Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital.
Several different types of peptides are naturally found in the body, like insulin and endorphins. Peptides can also be synthesized in labs, according to Harvard Health Publishing. GLP-1s, like Ozempic, are FDA-approved synthetic peptides, Dempsey says.
Injectable variations of synthetic peptides that haven't been approved by the FDA — such as BPC-157 and GHK-Cu, the latter of which has been marketed as a potential anti-aging drug — are the peptides that are making headlines at the moment, says Dr. Pieter Cohen, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School and internist at Cambridge Health Alliance.
Why are peptides gaining popularity among wellness influencers and some other consumers?
One likely factor behind synthetic peptides gaining more attention has been the success of drugs like Ozempic at addressing health concerns such as obesity and diabetes, according to Cohen. "That probably opened up [the idea that] there must be this magical world of these other peptides that we can have access to, that will do these sort of similar magical things in other areas," he says.
However, Cohen and other health experts have their concerns. After all, a compound's status as a peptide "doesn't mean it's close to Ozempic in any way, shape or form ... in terms of both its chemical structure or its effects on the human body," says Cohen.
Synthetic peptides advertised on social media and sold on the so-called gray market — often produced by overseas sellers and sold to U.S. consumers outside the normal American drug regulatory system — come with marketing claims such as boosting longevity, improving sleep quality, strengthening the immune system and even enhancing skin health and sexual function, according to Alexander.
Particularly among the people who consider GLP-1s a form of miracle drug, consumers may simply want to believe that the weight loss medicine's chemical cousins could have similar effects on other elements of human health. "Unfortunately, when it comes to peptides marketing, word of mouth has strongly surpassed where we are with any type of research," Dempsey says.
What do health experts recommend for consumers?
The health experts who spoke with CNBC Make It recommend against using any injectable peptides that aren't approved by the FDA, especially if you're unsure where or how they were produced. Always consult with a medical professional before making any major changes that can affect your health.
"My recommendation is not to use any of the novel, unstudied injectable peptides because we simply do not know if they work. And if they do work, if they're safe," Cohen says. When buying peptides on the gray market, you can receive entirely different compounds or doses, and some may be contaminated with bacteria or other concerning materials, he says.
"There's concerns both about the potential risks, but also about the unclear level of benefit from these products," Alexander says.
"We have a great regulatory system governing prescription drugs in the United States," Alexander adds. "For advocates of these products that really believe in them, I hope that they'll put their money where their mouth is, and do the studies that are necessary so that we can understand the true safety and effectiveness of the products."

articles.title: After SpaceX restores high-speed service, Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink agreement
articles.text:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Saturday said the company restricted Ukraine's access to its high-speed technology because Kyiv violated Starlink's terms of service.
In a post on X, Musk said: "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
He added: "SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR."
Ukraine officials said earlier in the day that SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems had restored high-speed service, a day after they said the service remained throttled. Ukrainian official said the service disruption left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks.
"The monitoring systems of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine officially record the restoration of the speed of Starlink/Starshield," it said in a statement. "The connection remains stable [while equipment is moving] at speeds over 400 km/h (249 miles per hour)."
"Previously, monitoring systems recorded limitations in the operation of Starlink/Starshield. Now the speed indicators have been restored," the ministry added.
Starlink is SpaceX's broader commercial satellite internet network, while Starshield is the company's government operations built on Starlink technology.
Before Musk's announcement, confusion lingered over who ordered the high-speed service restrictions, with Musk initially claiming in a social media post the U.S. government was responsible, while President Donald Trump had said he had no knowledge of it.
On Saturday, speaking to White House reporters in Florida, Trump confirmed a Wall Street Journal report this week that said he had asked Musk to ease the restrictions: "I have spoken to Elon Musk."
SpaceX did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade offering of its Starlink satellite internet service. Officials said any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions.
Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.
'Things have become harder'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on."
"Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said it continues to monitor the systems' operations.
"This result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," Defense Minister Yevgeny Khmara said in the statement.
Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties have called for a formal probe into Musk and SpaceX over alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.

articles.title: Goldman says these top tech stocks have plenty of upside ahead of earnings
articles.text: There are plenty of tech stocks to buy heading into their quarterly reports, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs. The investment bank sees companies including Microsoft offering more room to run. Other buy-rated stocks that Goldman Sachs recommends and that were screened by CNBC Pro include: Alphabet, Zeta Global, Palantir and CoreWeave. Microsoft There's alot to like about Microsoft, analyst Gabriela Borges, said ahead of the XBox maker's earnings on October 28. "We believe discovery value now shifts to the breadth and depth of Microsoft's AI platform; and unit economics and [return on invested capital] in Azure," she said. Goldman likes Microsoft's capex "flexibility" amid robust consumer demand for AI products and services. "We think Microsoft is the best positioned name in our Software coverage (also on ]Conviction List]) to benefit from compounding AI product cycles," she added. Shares are up more than 8% this year, lagging the more than 11% gain in the S & P 500. Zeta Global The marketing technology company was recently upgraded to buy from neutral at Goldman. "Zeta is benefiting from enterprise share gains as customers modernize legacy marketing platforms and consolidate fragmented data, intelligence and activation tools," analyst Callie Valenti wrote. The bank also said that while shares are up 67% this year, the stock still has plenty more room to run ahead of its next scheduled earnings in November. "Our industry conversations suggest that enterprises are prioritizing AI investments and increasingly evaluating where existing software spend can be consolidated, which should benefit Zeta's platform breadth and differentiated consumer data," Valenti went on. Alphabet Analyst Eric Sheridan is sticking with the Google and TouTube owner giant ahead of earnings next Wednesday. In a note to clients, Sheridan acknowledged some shareholder jitters but said they are mostly overdone. "...Investor concerns have increasingly centered on Search revenue growth, the absence to-date of a formal consumer agent launch, and the company's positioning should consumer behavior migrate toward agentic interfaces," he wrote. Still, Sheridan believes clients need to remain patient and keep buying the stock, which is only up 2% this year. Goldman went on to express confidence in Alphabet's AI vision as well as its ability to produce consumer applications "which together represent possible catalysts that could help shift the near-term narrative more constructively." Palantir "We believe agreements with the U.S. government can act as a growth driver as DoD modernization accelerates. These programs indicate that Palantir is moving deeper into mission critical workflows as DoD modernizes legacy systems and expands its use of commercial software and AI." Read more. Microsoft "We believe discovery value now shifts to the breadth & depth of Microsoft's AI platform; & unit economics & ROIC in Azure ... MSFT appears to have control over more variables in their capex equation today (which in turn drives more flexibility) ... We think Microsoft is the best positioned name in our Software coverage to benefit from compounding AI product cycles." CoreWeave "We recognize the challenges with forecasting out further in time, and in particular, predicting when supply/demand will ultimately normalize and the implications for residual value. However, we believe that datapoints in the next 12 months are likely to be positive for CoreWeave, and we would use this recent correction as an opportunity to buy the stock." Zeta Global "Zeta is benefiting from enterprise share gains as customers modernize legacy marketing platforms and consolidate fragmented data, intelligence, and activation tools. Our industry conversations suggest that enterprises are prioritizing AI investments and increasingly evaluating where existing software spend can be consolidated, which should benefit Zeta's platform breadth and differentiated consumer data." Alphabet "... Investor concerns have increasingly centered on Search revenue growth, the absence to-date of a formal consumer agent launch & company's positioning should consumer behavior migrate toward agentic interfaces ... we would highlight that we see GOOGL's AI strategy as broad-based anchored around frontier model development, GOOGL Cloud and consumer applications – which together represent possible catalysts that could help shift the near-term narrative more constructively."

articles.title: Berkshire shares shake the Buffett blues with new all-time highs
articles.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire shares shake the Buffett blues with new all-time highs
After almost 18 months, Berkshire Hathaway shares have entirely erased all the ground they lost in the wake of Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
On Friday, May 2, 2025, the Class A shares closed at $809,350. The Class B shares finished at $539.80.
Both were record-high closes.
The meeting was the following day, Saturday, May 3.
On Monday, May 5, BRK.A dropped 4.9% and BRK.B lost 5.1%.
CNBC.com noted a 14% drop in Q1 operating earnings, also announced that Saturday, may have contributed to the declines.
It also relayed some reassurance from analysts like Brian Meredith at UBS who predicted the company's culture and strategy would "remain unchanged" under new CEO Greg Abel.
"Buffett leaves a company that is less reliant on his investing capabilities, with an array of leading businesses with strong cash flows."
Investors, however, were apparently not reassured.
As the stock fell, there were fears a "Buffett premium" was evaporating.
Three months later, at their lowest closes of the year, BRK.A had lost 14.3% of its value and the more widely held B shares were down almost 15%.
Since then, they've rallied by 18%, and on Tuesday this week both classes topped their pre-announcement levels to set fresh all-time closing highs.
They were higher still on Thursday, setting new closing highs of $820,500 and $546.97.
Friday they lost almost 1% but remain roughly one-half of a percentage point above their highs just before the 2025 meeting.
Berkshire's gains have reduced its year-to-date deficit against the benchmark S&P to less than four percentage points.
October sprint
A majority of the net gain in points between the August 2025 low and now has been racked up this month.
Berkshire's B shares have gained almost 9% since the start of October, strongly outperforming the S&P 500's dip of 0.4% and an almost 4.8% drop for the equal-weight NYSE Fang+ index, which tracks 10 megacap tech names, including Meta, NVIDIA, and Alphabet.
Investors have been rotating out of high-flying tech and AI stocks in recent weeks amid growing concerns their massive spending on computing infrastructure won't produce the sustained profits they envision.
Berkshire, by contrast, is "the ultimate anti-AI play," according to a Barron's headline this week.
"With more than $350 billion in cash and equivalents on its balance sheet and close to $50 billion of annual after-tax earnings from a diverse group of businesses, Berkshire arguably is the most defensive megacap stock in the market."
And on CNBC's "Morning Call" Monday morning, Adam Patti of VistaShares, which runs an ETF that tracks Berkshire's portfolio, said the market's turn away from its long-running "momentum-driven frenzy" comes at a good time.
"The market spent a year pricing Berkshire without Buffett. I think it's finally decided Abel can, in fact, run it" and likes that he's taking advantage of the company's cash.
"Berkshire is a coiled spring. When it comes back, it comes back fast and furious."
But, as Patti notes, Berkshire isn't completely separated from the AI world.
CEO Greg Abel has said providing energy to the growing number of AI data centers is a "significant opportunity for Berkshire and Berkshire Hathaway Energy" as long as rates don't rise for its other customers.
And Berkshire has a now $34 billion position in Alphabet, one of AI's biggest players.
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET

HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Berkshire's hidden multi-billion-dollar mistakes (2001)
Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett admit their biggest errors are often "mistakes of omission" that don't appear in Berkshire's balance sheet.
AUDIENCE MEMBER: Mr. Munger, I know you're fond of evoking humility to promote rational thought. So my question is, what's the most recent business mistake that you've made, Mr. Munger, and why did it occur? (Laughter)
WARREN BUFFETT: I'm going to take notes on this one. (Laughter)
CHARLIE MUNGER: The mistakes that have been most extreme in Berkshire's history are mistakes of omission. They don't show up in our figures. They show up in opportunity costs.
In other words, we have opportunities, we almost do it. In retrospect, we can tell that we were very much mistaken not to do it.
In terms of the shareholders, those are the ones in our history that it really cost the most. And very few managements do much thinking or talking about opportunity costs.
But Warren, we have blown —
WARREN BUFFETT: Billions and billions and billions. I might as well say it. (Laughter)
CHARLIE MUNGER: Right, right. And we keep doing it. (Laughter)
WARREN BUFFETT: Some might say we're getting better at it. (Laughter)
CHARLIE MUNGER: I don't like mentioning the specific companies, because the — you know, we may, in due course, want to buy them again and have an opportunity to do so at our price.
But practically everywhere in life, and in corporate life, too, what really costs, in comparison with what easily might have been, are the blown opportunities. I mean, it just — it's an awesome amount of money...
WARREN BUFFETT: I might add that when we speak of errors of omission, of which we've had plenty, and some very big ones, we don't mean not buying some stock where we — a friend runs it, or we know the name and it went from one to 100. That doesn't mean anything. It's only —
We only regard errors as being things that are within our circle of competence.
So if somebody knows how to make money in cocoa beans, or they know how to make money in a software company or anything, and we miss that, that is not an error, as far as we're concerned.
What's an error is when it's something we understand, and we stand there and stare at it, and we don't do anything.
Or worse yet, what really gets me is when we do something very small with it. We do an eyedropper's worth of it, when we could do it very big.
Charlie refers to that elegantly when I do that sort of thing as when I'm sucking my thumb. (Laughter)
And there really — I mean, we have been thumbsuckers at times with businesses that we understood well.
And it may have been because we started buying, and the price moved up a little, and we waited around hoping we would get more at the price we originally started — there could be a lot of things.
But those are huge mistakes. Conventional accounting, of course, does not pick those up at all. But they're in our scorebook.
